title: Spanish foundations
description: Fifty-two Spanish lessons covering A1-level material — first words, introductions, café requests, numbers, directions, shopping, time and days, family, home and daily routine, everyday exchanges, getting around, past and future plans, weather and time-telling, months and dates, the market, free time, health and social life — plus seventeen A2 lessons in five units — El pasado (preterite, imperfect, choosing between them, weekend narratives), El futuro (future formation and uses, plans and intentions), Deseos y cortesía (conditional, polite requests, first subjunctive), Conectar frases (relative clauses, comparatives, object pronouns, por vs para), and Trabajo y tecnología (superlatives, a hotel check-in mission, tech talk). CEFR level tagging is partial, and native-speaker editorial review remains open for the whole pack; lessons are machine-authored and consistency-checked.

concepts.title: First words and greetings
concepts.explanation: Spanish greets by the hour, and it greets in the plural even for a single morning: buenos días, buenas tardes. The habit worth starting on day one is that Spanish marks a question twice, with an upside-down question mark at the front and an ordinary one at the end, so you can see a question coming before you have read a word of it.
concepts.commonError: Say hola the moment you arrive. Save adiós for leaving.

concepts.title: Introducing yourself
concepts.explanation: Spanish says Me llamo Ana, literally 'I call myself Ana'; the verb llamarse carries a pronoun that points back at the speaker. Asking the same question of someone else changes that pronoun to te: ¿Cómo te llamas? Soy Ana is the plain alternative, built on 'to be'.
concepts.commonError: Use me llamo for your own name and te llamas in the informal question. Do not swap me and te.

concepts.title: Polite café requests
concepts.explanation: For a polite café request Spanish uses quisiera, 'I would like', instead of the blunter quiero: Quisiera un café, por favor. The article stays un for either drink, and café and té keep their accents.

examples.meaning: I would like a coffee, please.
I would like a tea, please.

concepts.commonError: Keep un with café and té in these requests. Remember the accents in café and té.

concepts.title: Numbers and quantities
concepts.explanation: Spanish runs one to ten as ordinary digits, then glues the parts of a number together where English keeps them apart: dieciséis for sixteen, veintiuno for twenty-one. That gluing stops at thirty, where a separate y appears, treinta y uno. A number in front of a noun also has to agree with it: un café is one coffee, but una manzana is one apple.

examples.meaning: How much does a coffee cost?

concepts.commonError: Use cuánto for the price of one item. Keep una with manzana because it is feminine.

concepts.title: Asking the way
concepts.explanation: Spanish marks the asking word with a written accent: dónde asks 'where', while the same letters without it, donde, are not asking anything. The accent does not change how the word sounds; it tells you what the word is doing, and a direct question also opens with ¿ and closes with ?. Ask about a place with estar, ¿Dónde está la estación?, and learn the directions as chunks: todo recto, a la izquierda, a la derecha, with luego joining the second step to the first.

examples.target: Todo recto, luego a la izquierda.
examples.meaning: Straight ahead, then to the left.
Excuse me, where is the bathroom?

concepts.commonError: Dónde asks where. Quién asks who and qué asks what. The accent on dónde marks the question and drops in the middle of a sentence.

concepts.title: Prices and paying
concepts.explanation: A Spanish question wears two marks, an upside-down one at the front and an ordinary one at the end, so ¿Cuánto cuesta? announces itself before you read a word. Costar changes its stem under stress: cuesta for a single item, cuestan for several, and never costa. The bill is la cuenta, a feminine noun, and por favor is the politeness that travels with it.

examples.meaning: How much does the coffee cost?

concepts.commonError: Spanish puts no before the verb, never after it. Cost is cuesta for one thing and cuestan for several.

concepts.title: Days and times
concepts.explanation: Five Spanish weekdays are the old sky names — lunes (moon), martes (Mars), miércoles (Mercury), jueves (Jupiter), viernes (Venus) — while sábado and domingo come from the Sabbath and the Lord’s day. They are masculine and lower-case, and the article el carries the meaning of ‘on’: el lunes. Mañana is tomorrow; la mañana is the morning.
concepts.commonError: Mañana is both tomorrow and morning. La mañana is the morning; mañana alone in a schedule usually means tomorrow.

concepts.title: Family and people
concepts.explanation: Spanish shows a noun's gender in its article — el hermano, la hermana — and hides an irregular verb under the simplest sentence: yo tengo, never yo tene. The possessive mi does not change with who is speaking; it changes with how many people are being counted, so mi hermana is one sister and mis hermanas is two, whoever the speaker is.
concepts.commonError: Tengo, not tene. Tener is irregular in the I form and it is the form you use most when talking about family.

concepts.title: Home and articles
concepts.explanation: Every Spanish noun is masculine or feminine, and the article shows it: el dormitorio, la cocina. In the plural the articles become los and las. Two little contractions do heavy work: a + el becomes al, as in voy al baño, and de + el becomes del, as in vengo del salón.

examples.meaning: I come from the living room.

concepts.commonError: Never write a el or de el — the contraction is obligatory: al baño, del salón.

concepts.title: Describing people and things
concepts.explanation: Ser describes what something is like: El libro es nuevo. The adjective copies the noun's gender and number — alto for a masculine noun, alta for a feminine one, altos and altas in the plural. Muy simply turns the volume up: muy grande.
concepts.commonError: The adjective must match the noun it describes, not the speaker: una mesa nueva, never una mesa nuevo.

concepts.title: More than one
concepts.explanation: The plural is almost always one step: add -s after a vowel — libro becomes libros, mesa becomes mesas. After a consonant, add -es — flor becomes flores, and lápiz changes its z to c: lápices. The article changes too: el becomes los, la becomes las.
concepts.commonError: After a consonant the plural needs -es, never just -s: flores, not flors.

concepts.title: Work and daily routine
concepts.explanation: Most Spanish verbs are regular: drop the -ar and add -o for I, -a for he or she — trabajo, trabaja. Estudiar works the same way: estudio, estudia. The day divides into three parts with por: por la mañana, por la tarde, por la noche.

examples.target: Mi hermano trabaja por la noche.

concepts.commonError: Por la mañana is a fixed phrase — never en la mañana.

concepts.title: Saying no
concepts.explanation: To negate, put no directly before the verb: No trabajo. Spanish also loves negative words that team up with no: nunca (never), nada (nothing), nadie (nobody). No como nada is perfectly correct — the two negatives strengthen each other instead of cancelling out.
concepts.commonError: No must stand before the verb — Trabajo no is not Spanish.

concepts.title: Asking questions
concepts.explanation: Question words carry a written accent that tells them apart from their twins: qué (what) versus que (that), dónde (where) versus donde (where, as a connector). After the question word, the verb usually comes before the subject: ¿Dónde trabaja Ana? ¿Qué estudias?
concepts.commonError: The accent is the meaning: ¿Como te llamas? would read as I eat your name.

concepts.title: Food and drink
concepts.explanation: Comer and beber are regular -er verbs: como, comes, come; bebo, bebes, bebe. Liking works backwards in Spanish: instead of I like the bread, Spanish says the bread is pleasing to me — Me gusta el pan. With a plural noun the verb becomes plural too: Me gustan las frutas.
concepts.commonError: Gustar agrees with the thing liked, not with you: Me gusta el pan, never Me gusto el pan.

concepts.title: Mine and yours
concepts.explanation: Mi, tu and su sit before the noun and never change for gender: mi libro, mi casa. They do change for number: mis libros, tus casas. Su is the busy one — it can mean his, her, your (formal) or their, and context does the sorting.
concepts.commonError: The possessive copies the noun's number, not the owner's: mis libros even though there is only one of me.

concepts.title: Getting around
concepts.explanation: Ir (to go) is irregular but tiny: voy, vas, va, vamos, van. The transport goes after en — en coche, en metro, en autobús — with one rebel: a pie, on foot. To say where, use a: Voy al centro, from al = a + el.

examples.target: Va a la escuela a pie.
examples.meaning: He/She goes to school on foot.

concepts.commonError: Transport takes en, never con: en metro, not con metro.

concepts.title: Polite requests
concepts.explanation: Poder (can) and querer (want) are followed by the infinitive: Puedo ir, Quiero comer. Their forms: puedo, puedes, puede and quiero, quieres, quiere. For extra politeness, Spanish reaches for the conditional: Querría un café, por favor — I would like a coffee, please.

examples.meaning: I would like the bill, please.

concepts.commonError: After poder and querer comes the plain infinitive — Puedo ir, never Puedo voy.

concepts.title: Yesterday: a first look at the past
concepts.explanation: The pretérito talks about finished actions: for -ar verbs add -é for I — hablé, trabajé, estudié. For -er and -ir verbs add -í — comí, viví. Then there's fue, which does double duty as was and went. Anchor it all with ayer (yesterday) and anoche (last night).
concepts.commonError: The accent is the past: hablo is I speak, hablé is I spoke.

concepts.title: Making plans
concepts.explanation: The near future is simply ir a plus the infinitive: Voy a cocinar, Vas a venir, Van a estudiar. It works for tonight, tomorrow, or next year — Spanish doesn't fuss about how near near is. Pair it with time words like mañana or este fin de semana.
concepts.commonError: The a is not optional: Voy cocinar is missing its bridge — Voy a cocinar.

concepts.title: Weather and seasons
concepts.explanation: Spanish makes the weather with hacer: Hace sol, Hace frío, Hace calor. For cloudy or rainy skies it switches to estar: Está nublado. The seasons are la primavera, el verano, el otoño, el invierno — and they're handy for small talk: En verano hace calor.
concepts.commonError: Weather takes hace, not es: Hace frío, never Es frío.

concepts.title: Telling the time
concepts.explanation: Ask with ¿Qué hora es? One o'clock is special: Es la una. Every other hour uses son: Son las dos, Son las diez. Half past is y media, quarter past is y cuarto, and quarter to counts backwards: menos cuarto.
concepts.commonError: It's Es la una but Son las dos — the verb agrees with the hour.

concepts.title: Months and dates
concepts.explanation: The twelve months are masculine and always lowercase: enero, mayo, diciembre. Dates put the day first with el: el 3 de mayo, el 20 de diciembre. For birthdays, the pattern is Mi cumpleaños es el 5 de enero — or simply en junio for the month alone.

examples.target: La fiesta es el 20 de diciembre.

concepts.commonError: Months are never capitalised in Spanish: en junio, not en Junio.

concepts.title: At the market
concepts.explanation: Quantities pair with de: un kilo de manzanas, una botella de agua, medio kilo de queso. To point at something near you, use este for masculine and esta for feminine: Este pan está fresco, Esta fruta es buena.

examples.target: Medio kilo de queso, por favor.
examples.meaning: Half a kilo of cheese, please.

concepts.commonError: The quantity needs its de: un kilo de manzanas, never un kilo manzanas.

concepts.title: Free time and hobbies
concepts.explanation: Hobbies love the infinitive: Me gusta leer, Me encanta nadar. With an infinitive, gustar always stays singular — the action counts as one thing. For stronger feelings there's encantar: Me encanta el cine. And sports take jugar: Juego al fútbol, with al fusing a + el.
concepts.commonError: With two infinitives gustar still stays singular: Me gusta leer y nadar.

concepts.title: Health and the body
concepts.explanation: Pain in Spanish works like liking: Me duele la cabeza — the head hurts to me. One body part takes duele, several take duelen: Me duelen las manos. Note the article, not the possessive: la cabeza, never mi cabeza. For care, Voy al médico.

examples.meaning: I'm going to the doctor tomorrow.

concepts.commonError: Body parts take the article: Me duele la cabeza, not Me duele mi cabeza.

concepts.title: At the pharmacy
concepts.explanation: Necesito opens every request: Necesito estas pastillas. Ask the pharmacist with ¿Tiene algo para…?: ¿Tiene algo para el dolor de cabeza? Para marks purpose — for the pain — where por would mean because of it. Useful to hear: Es sin receta, no prescription needed.

examples.target: ¿Tiene algo para el dolor de cabeza?
examples.meaning: Do you have something for a headache?

concepts.commonError: Purpose takes para: algo para el dolor, never algo por el dolor.

concepts.title: Emergencies
concepts.explanation: ¡Socorro! is the cry for help; ¡Ayuda! works too. In a real emergency, use the formal command: ¡Llame a una ambulancia! Llame is the usted form — emergencies are no place for informality. Ask ¿Dónde está el hospital? or ¿Dónde hay un hospital?

examples.target: Llame a una ambulancia, por favor.

concepts.commonError: Emergencies use the formal command: Llame, not the informal Llama.

concepts.title: Invitations
concepts.explanation: Te invito a… opens the invitation: Te invito a cenar. Ask ¿Quieres venir? or ¿Vienes a la fiesta? Accept warmly with ¡Claro que sí! Decline softly with Lo siento, no puedo — sorry, I can't — which keeps the door open.
concepts.commonError: Invitar takes a: Te invito a cenar, never Te invito cenar.

concepts.title: El pretérito: las formas
concepts.explanation: The pretérito reports finished actions. Habit first: anchor every past verb to a finished moment — ayer, anoche, el sábado. Pattern second: -ar endings -é/-aste/-ó, -er/-ir endings -í/-iste/-ió, and a small gang of irregulars (tuve, hice, dije, estuvo, fue) that ignore the pattern completely.
concepts.commonError: Present endings in a past story (*Hablo ayer) break the spell. Ayer forces the past: Ayer hablé. Watch the accent — hablo is I speak, hablé is I spoke.

concepts.title: El imperfecto: el pasado en curso
concepts.explanation: The imperfecto describes what was ongoing or habitual: settings (era de noche), habits (jugaba cada día), background (mientras cenábamos). Habit first: if you can add 'used to' or 'was -ing' in English, reach for the imperfecto. Pattern second: -aba for -ar, -ía for -er/-ir; only era, iba, veía break it.

examples.meaning: As a kid I used to play football.

examples.target: Había mucha gente en la plaza.
examples.meaning: There were a lot of people in the square.
While we were having dinner, the phone rang.

concepts.commonError: Don't use the pretérito for background: *Fue una tarde tranquila sounds like the calm ended on schedule. A scene that simply was → Era una tarde tranquila.

concepts.title: Elegir el pasado: evento o fondo
concepts.explanation: Two pasts, two jobs. Pretérito = what happened, finished and counted (llovió, sonó, vi). Imperfecto = what was happening, the background film (llovía, dormía, jugaba). Habit first: ask 'did it finish, or was it ongoing?' Pattern second: finished-time words (ayer, una vez, de repente) → pretérito; habitual words (siempre, todos los días, de niño, mientras) → imperfecto.

examples.meaning: Last week it rained a lot.
As a child it used to rain a lot.
While I was sleeping, the phone rang.

examples.target: Una vez vi una película genial.
examples.meaning: Once I saw a great movie.

concepts.commonError: Don't let a finished time word wear the imperfecto: *La semana pasada llovía treats one finished week as an endless habit. Finished frame → llovió.

concepts.title: Narrar el fin de semana
concepts.explanation: A weekend story runs on two rails: time anchors (el sábado, por la mañana, el domingo) and finished verbs (fui, vimos, descansé). Habit first: say when, then say what — the anchor licenses the past tense. Pattern second: primero → después → por último chains the events in order.

examples.meaning: On Saturday I went to the market.

examples.target: Por la tarde vimos una película.
examples.meaning: In the afternoon we watched a movie.
On Sunday I rested at home.

examples.target: Primero desayuné, después salí a correr.
examples.meaning: First I had breakfast, then I went out for a run.

concepts.commonError: Don't narrate finished events in the present: *El sábado voy al cine describes a habit, not last Saturday. It happened → El sábado fui al cine.

concepts.title: El futuro simple: las formas
concepts.explanation: The futuro simple predicts and promises. Habit first: attach it to tomorrow-words — mañana, el lunes, la próxima semana. Pattern second: whole infinitive + é/ás/á/emos/án, identical for -ar, -er and -ir. Six stems rebel: tener→tendr-, poder→podr-, hacer→har-, decir→dir-, venir→vendr-, salir→saldr-.

examples.meaning: Tomorrow I will speak with him.
I will have time on Friday.
I will do the homework tonight.

concepts.commonError: Don't conjugate first and then add: *hablo + é is wrong. The future keeps the whole infinitive — hablar + é = hablaré.

concepts.title: Para qué sirve el futuro
concepts.explanation: Three habits, one tense. Promise: te llamaré, vendré — the speaker commits. Prediction: lloverá, será — the speaker forecasts, often boosted by creo que/probablemente/seguro. Supposition: estará en casa — the future guesses about the present. Habit first: hear the intention behind the verb, not just the time.

examples.meaning: He must be at home now.

concepts.commonError: Don't use the future for a plan you already decided and booked: Mañana *viajaré sounds like a forecast. Decided plan → Voy a viajar. The future predicts; ir a executes.

concepts.title: Ir a + infinitivo: los planes
concepts.explanation: Ir a + infinitive is the near future of decided plans: voy a, vas a, va a, vamos a. Habit first: if you could add 'I've decided' in English, use ir a. Pattern second: conjugate ir, add a, keep the second verb untouched. Querer names the wish behind the plan: Quiero viajar.

examples.meaning: I am going to study medicine.
Are you going to come to the party?
We are going to buy a house.

concepts.commonError: Don't stack them: *Voy a querer is clumsy. A wish is Quiero; a decided plan is Voy a + verb. One job per construction.

concepts.title: El condicional: would
concepts.explanation: The condicional imagines: wishes (me gustaría), advice (deberías), polite requests (¿podrías?). Habit first: if English says would/could/should, reach for the condicional. Pattern second: infinitive + ía/ías/ía/íamos/ían — the future's endings with the stress moved. Same six rebel stems as the future: podría, tendría, haría, diría, vendría, saldría.

examples.meaning: I would like to travel to Japan.
It would be great to see you.

concepts.commonError: Don't use the future for would: *Me gustará viajar means I will like traveling — a prediction, not a wish. Would needs the -ía ending: Me gustaría.

concepts.title: Pedir con cortesía
concepts.explanation: To ask like a local, borrow would: Me gustaría + noun/infinitive, Quisiera + noun/infinitive. Habit first: in shops, restaurants and hotels, start every request with one of them — never the bare imperative. Pattern second: Me gustaría una mesa; Quisiera la cuenta; ¿Sería tan amable de ayudarme?

examples.target: Me gustaría una mesa para dos.
examples.meaning: I would like a table for two.
I would like to speak with the manager.
Would you be so kind as to help me?
I would love to come back.

concepts.commonError: Don't order with the imperative among strangers: *Dame la cuenta barks. Quisiera la cuenta, por favor asks — and gets a smile.

concepts.title: El subjuntivo tras quiero que
concepts.explanation: Two subjects, one wish → the second verb goes subjunctive: Quiero (I) que vengas (you). Habit first: hear quiero que / necesito que / es importante que as an alarm bell — the next verb changes. Pattern second: yo-present minus -o plus opposite endings (hable, coma, viva); key forms: vengas, hables, quiera, pueda, sea, digas.

examples.target: Quiero que vengas a la fiesta.
examples.meaning: I want you to come to the party.
I need you to help me.
I want you to speak more slowly.

concepts.commonError: Don't keep the indicative after que: *Quiero que vienes is the classic mistake. One wisher, one other person → the second verb must be subjunctive: Quiero que vengas.

concepts.title: Oraciones de relativo
concepts.explanation: Relative words replace a whole second sentence. Habit first: need to add information about a noun? Reach for que — it covers things, people (without preposition) and ideas. Pattern second: person + preposition → quien/quienes (con quien hablé); place → donde (donde vivo); the-one-that → el que; what/that-which → lo que.

examples.target: El libro que leí es genial.
examples.meaning: The book (that) I read is great.

examples.target: La persona con quien hablé fue amable.
examples.meaning: The person with whom I spoke was kind.

examples.target: La ciudad donde vivo es pequeña.
examples.meaning: The city where I live is small.

concepts.commonError: Don't use que for people after a preposition: *la persona con que hablé is wrong. People + preposition → con quien.

concepts.title: Comparar: más, menos, tan… como
concepts.explanation: Habit first: comparing two things? más/menos + adjective + que. Saying they're equal? tan + adjective + como. Pattern second: bueno→mejor, malo→peor, grande→mayor, pequeño→menor — the four rebels replace the whole formula. Before a number, que becomes de: más de tres.

examples.target: Madrid es más grande que Sevilla.
Mi piso es menos caro que el tuyo.
examples.meaning: My flat is less expensive than yours.

examples.target: Es tan alto como su hermano.
examples.meaning: He is as tall as his brother.

concepts.commonError: Don't stack comparisons: *más mejor is wrong — mejor already contains the 'more'. One comparison per sentence.

concepts.title: Pronombres de objeto
concepts.explanation: Habit first: about to repeat a noun? Replace it. Lo/la = him/her/it (direct: what you see, buy, give). Le/les = to him/her/them (indirect: who receives). Pattern second: pronouns go before the conjugated verb (Lo veo, Le di); two pronouns together go indirect-then-direct, and le+lo melts into se lo.

examples.target: Le di el libro a María.
examples.meaning: I gave the book to María.
He gave it to me yesterday.

concepts.commonError: Don't keep both: *Le lo di is wrong — le + lo melts into se lo: Se lo di. Se is the diplomat that prevents le-lo collisions.

concepts.title: Por o para
concepts.explanation: Habit first: explaining a cause or moving through space → por. Naming a goal, a recipient or a deadline → para. Pattern second: por = because of / through / in exchange for (por eso, por aquí, gracias por); para = in order to / for (a recipient) / by (a deadline) (para aprender, para ti, para mañana).
concepts.commonError: Don't swap them: *Estudio por aprender is wrong — purpose is para: Estudio para aprender. Por explains what already happened; para points at what's next.

concepts.title: El superlativo
concepts.explanation: Habit first: crowning one above all? el/la/los/las + más + adjective + de: el más alto de la clase. Going extreme? -ísimo on the adjective: buenísimo, rapidísimo. Pattern second: the article must match the noun (los más amables); -ísimo drops the adjective's final vowel (bueno→buenísimo, grande→grandísima).

examples.target: Es el más alto de la clase.
examples.meaning: He is the tallest in the class.
She is a really good person.

concepts.commonError: Don't forget the article: *Es más alto de la clase is just a comparison with a missing rival. The crown needs el: Es el más alto de la clase.

concepts.title: Misión: en el hotel
concepts.explanation: Checking in is a script: greet, confirm the reservation, get the key, ask about breakfast. When something breaks, the magic frame is No hay… — No hay agua caliente, no hay toallas. Report, don't apologize: name what's missing and the desk will fix it.

examples.target: Tengo una reserva a nombre de García.
examples.meaning: I have a reservation under García.

examples.target: Aquí tiene la llave de su habitación.

concepts.commonError: Don't say *Tengo una reservación — the word is reserva. And it's la llave, feminine even though it ends in -e.

concepts.title: Hablar de tecnología
concepts.explanation: Habit first: tech problems are reported with estar + adjective (está rota, no funciona) and fixed with regular verbs (enciende, descarga, envía). Pattern second: most tech nouns are masculine (el móvil, el ordenador, el wifi); asking for the password is always ¿Cuál es la contraseña de…? with del before masculine nouns.

examples.meaning: I'll send you the document now.

concepts.commonError: Don't translate word by word: *la contraseña de el wifi is wrong. De + el always contracts: la contraseña del wifi.

vocabulary.example: Todo recto, luego a la izquierda.
Todo recto, luego a la izquierda.
La mesa está en la cocina.

vocabulary.meaning: I/he/she was going / used to go

vocabulary.example: Todos los días iba al parque.
El fin de semana fue genial.
Por la tarde leí un libro.
Quiero que me digas la verdad.

activities.body: It is 10 a.m. in Madrid. You find a seat at a café, and the server comes over. Greet them, ask for un café, and thank them when it arrives. Read the three lines below, then try the exchange yourself.

activities.prompt: The server reaches your table. How do you greet them?
hints: The server spoke to you first, so you answer with a greeting — the one-word line that means 'hello'.
activities.feedback: Hola opens the exchange.

activities.prompt: Build the order: A coffee, please.
hints: The request starts with the article un, then the drink café, and por favor closes it — one line: Un café, por favor.
activities.feedback: Un café, por favor. Keep the request together as one line.

activities.prompt: The cup reaches your table. What do you say?
hints: The order is over and the coffee has arrived — pick the line that closes the exchange by thanking the server.
activities.feedback: Gracias closes the exchange.

activities.prompt: Say the order once in your head. Then write in Spanish: A coffee, please.
hints: It is the same three-word line you just built: un ('a') + café + por favor.
activities.feedback: You wrote the order without the tiles.

errors.explanation: The request needs the small un ('a') in front of café: Un café, por favor.
Por favor is the polite part that makes the request courteous — keep it: Un café, por favor.
Porfavor is not one word — por favor is two separate words.

activities.prompt: Match the three lines you used to their meanings.
hints: Each Spanish line has exactly one English twin — Gracias is the one that means 'thank you'.
activities.feedback: You can recognize the whole exchange.

activities.prompt: Write the three lines in order: Hello. / A coffee, please. / Thank you.
hints: Follow the order of the mission: greet first (Hola.), then the request (Un café, por favor.), then thank the server (Gracias.).
activities.feedback: You greeted, ordered, and thanked the server.

answers: Hola. Un café, por favor. Gracias.

errors.explanation: The polite request keeps por favor: Un café, por favor.
'A coffee' needs its article un in front of café.

activities.body: Spanish does not say 'my name is'. It says Me llamo Ana, literally 'I call myself Ana' — the small me is part of the verb llamarse and points back at the speaker. Turn the same verb on the person in front of you and that me becomes te: ¿Cómo te llamas? Soy Ana is the other introduction, and that one uses plain 'to be'. The pronoun, not the verb, is what changes.

activities.prompt: Me llamo Ana and Soy Ana both give a name. Which one uses the verb that literally means 'I call myself'?
hints: The reflexive verb is llamarse — the option built on me llamo is the one that literally says 'I call myself'.
activities.feedback: Me llamo Ana is the reflexive form — 'I call myself Ana'. Soy Ana uses ser ('to be'), and ¿Cómo te llamas? is the question.

activities.prompt: Ask a classmate their name with the question whose pronoun changes to te.
hints: It starts with ¿Cómo ('how'), then the pronoun te, then the verb llamas — the question form of the same verb from Me llamo.
activities.feedback: The verb is the same one as in Me llamo, but the pronoun turns into te when it points at the person you are speaking to.

errors.explanation: That is the self-introduction, not a question. Pointing at the other person turns the pronoun into te and the verb into llamas: ¿Cómo te llamas?
Me is for yourself; when you ask someone else the pronoun becomes te: ¿Cómo te llamas?
That is a word-for-word translation from English. Spanish asks 'how do you call yourself': ¿Cómo te llamas?

activities.prompt: Read the exchange. Which short word tells you the first speaker is talking about herself?
hints: Look at the first speaker's line: the two-letter word right before the verb llamo is the reflexive pronoun pointing back at Ana.
activities.feedback: Me is the reflexive pronoun: it turns the verb llamarse back on the person speaking. The other introduction uses soy instead.

errors.explanation: Soy is the verb of the other introduction ('I am Leo') — it has no reflexive pronoun. The first speaker's pronoun is the two-letter word before llamo.
Llamo is the verb, not the pronoun. The short word that turns it back on the speaker is me, right before it.

activities.prompt: A neighbour introduces herself to you. Give the two-word Spanish reply that closes an introduction.
hints: It is the fixed phrase from the examples that means 'nice to meet you' — two words, no verb, and it works for any speaker.
activities.feedback: Mucho gusto closes an introduction, and the sentence needs no pronoun.

errors.explanation: De nada means 'you're welcome' — it answers gracias, not an introduction. The two-word closer is Mucho gusto.
Encantada is also a polite closer (it agrees with the speaker's gender), but the two-word form this lesson teaches is Mucho gusto.

activities.prompt: The words are jumbled. Build the reflexive sentence that gives Ana's name.
hints: The reflexive pronoun comes first, then the verb, then the name: Me + llamo + Ana.
activities.feedback: Me llamo Ana puts the reflexive pronoun first, then the verb, then the name.

activities.prompt: A classmate has introduced herself. Introduce yourself the same way, as Ana, using the verb that needs a pronoun.
hints: Use the same three words you just built: the pronoun Me, then llamo, then the name Ana — the pronoun cannot be left out.
activities.feedback: Say the whole reflexive phrase; leaving out me would leave the verb belonging to nobody.

errors.explanation: The reflexive verb needs its pronoun: without me, the verb belongs to nobody. Say Me llamo Ana.
Soy Ana uses plain 'to be'. The prompt asks for the reflexive form with its pronoun: Me llamo Ana.

activities.body: Quiero means 'I want', and in a café it can sound blunt. Spanish softens the same verb into quisiera, 'I would like', and that ending is the whole difference: Quisiera un café, por favor. The article un does not change with the drink — Quisiera un té, por favor — so only the noun moves. Keep the accents: café and té each carry one, and por favor is the phrase that turns the request into a courteous one.

activities.prompt: Quiero and quisiera are the same verb. Which request is the softened, polite one?
hints: The polite form is the longer one that starts with Quis- and ends in -a — it sounds like 'key-syeh-rah'.
activities.feedback: Quisiera gives the verb a conditional ending, and that is what makes the request courteous. Quiero is the blunt form.

activities.prompt: Ask for tea politely, using the softened verb rather than quiero.
hints: Same frame as the café request: start with Quisiera, then un té (with the accent on té), and close with por favor.
activities.feedback: Same polite frame, tea instead of coffee: Quisiera un té, por favor, with the accent on té.

errors.explanation: Quiero is the blunt 'I want'. The softened form is quisiera — the same verb with the conditional ending.
Té carries an accent — without it, te means 'you', not 'tea'.
Keep the polite closer: Quisiera un té, por favor.

activities.prompt: Read the café exchange. How many drinks does the customer order?
hints: Count everything the customer asks for: the té in the first line, plus the extra drink added with 'y un café también' ('and a coffee too').
activities.feedback: The customer asks for a té and then adds un café, so two drinks in all.

errors.explanation: The first line asks for a té, but the customer comes back and adds un café too (y un café también) — two drinks in all.
There is more than one order: a té, then an added un café — two drinks in all.

activities.prompt: What does this café line mean in English: Quisiera un café, por favor.
hints: Quisiera is the polite 'I would like' (like 'I'd like'), un café is 'a coffee', and por favor is 'please'.
activities.feedback: Quisiera is 'I would like', and por favor supplies the 'please'.

answers: I would like a coffee, please.

errors.explanation: Quiero would mean 'I want'. The line uses quisiera, the polite 'I would like'.
The line keeps the polite verb at the front: 'I would like a coffee, please'.

activities.prompt: Put the words in order to build the polite request for one coffee.
hints: The polite verb comes first (Quisiera), then the drink with its article (un café), then the two-word closer (por favor).
activities.feedback: Quisiera opens it, the drink follows with un, and por favor finishes the request.

activities.prompt: You reach the counter and want a coffee. Make the short polite request, without the verb.
hints: Drop the verb entirely — simply name the drink with its article and add por favor: Un café, por favor.
activities.feedback: Un café, por favor — the short request drops quisiera but keeps por favor.

errors.explanation: The request needs its article: 'a coffee' is un café, por favor.
Keep the polite closer por favor — it is what makes the short request courteous.

activities.body: Spanish counts one to ten straight. The stretch that surprises English speakers is the twenties: veintiuno, veintidós, veintitrés, written as one word, the same way dieciséis and diecisiete glue their parts together. The separate y arrives only at thirty-one, treinta y uno. Because the number agrees with its noun, one is un with a masculine café and una with a feminine manzana.

activities.prompt: Three is hiding inside veintitrés, glued to veinte. Which Spanish word is it?
hints: Split veintitrés in half: veinti- carries the 'twenty', and the glued tail holds the number you already know from one to ten.
activities.feedback: Tres is three. The twenties simply glue a number onto veinte, so veintitrés is twenty-three.

activities.prompt: Read the price board. How much is the tea?
hints: Find the line that starts with Té — its price is the second one on the board: tres euros.
activities.feedback: The board prices tea at tres euros. Dos and tres behave here exactly as they did when you counted.

errors.explanation: Dos euros is the price of the coffee (Café: dos euros). The tea line reads Té: tres euros.

activities.prompt: Put the Spanish words in order to ask the price of one coffee.
hints: The inverted question mark opens the sentence with ¿Cuánto, the verb cuesta follows, then the drink with its article: un café.
activities.feedback: ¿Cuánto cuesta? is the price question as a unit, and the upside-down question mark opens the sentence. Un café follows it.

activities.prompt: Say in Spanish: Two apples, please.
hints: Dos works for any noun, manzanas is the plural of 'apple', and the polite closer por favor ends the line.
activities.feedback: Manzanas is feminine plural, so 'one' would be una, but two is dos either way, only the word for one changes with the noun.

errors.explanation: With dos ('two') the noun is plural: dos manzanas.
Una means 'one' — the prompt asks for two, which is dos: Dos manzanas, por favor.
End the request politely with por favor: Dos manzanas, por favor.

activities.prompt: Think: a fruit seller has one apple but no sign. Ask the price in Spanish, then write the question.
hints: Use the same price question from this lesson — ¿Cuánto cuesta — and make 'one apple' agree with the feminine noun: una manzana.
activities.feedback: One apple is una manzana, with the feminine una. The price question itself never changes.

errors.explanation: Manzana is feminine, so 'one' must be una, not un: ¿Cuánto cuesta una manzana?
The question needs the article before the noun: una manzana.

activities.prompt: Three of these give a direction; the fourth is asking. Which single word is the asking one?
hints: The asking word carries a written accent and means 'where'. The other three — izquierda, derecha, recto — tell you a way to go, and none of them asks anything.
activities.feedback: Dónde means where, and the written accent is there because the word is asking. Quién does the same job for a person, qué for a thing.

activities.prompt: Put the Spanish words in order to ask where the station is.
hints: The question opens with the asking word ¿Dónde, then the verb está, then the article la, then the place estación — exactly the order from the exchange you read.
activities.feedback: The question opens with ¿ and its asking word dónde, and estar supplies está. Estación is feminine, so its article is la.

activities.prompt: Ask in Spanish where the bathroom is. Baño is masculine.
hints: Keep the skeleton from the station question — ¿Dónde está + article + place. The prompt hands you the article: baño is masculine, so it takes el.
activities.feedback: Only the noun and its article change inside ¿Dónde está?; el marks the masculine baño. The accent on dónde stays, because the word is still asking.

errors.explanation: The article el has to sit between the verb and the place: ¿Dónde está el baño?
Location takes estar, not ser — a place is where it is: ¿Dónde está el baño?
The prompt marks baño as masculine, so its article is el, not la: ¿Dónde está el baño?
Estás means 'you are'. The question asks where the bathroom is — third person está: ¿Dónde está el baño?

activities.prompt: Complete the directions: Todo recto, luego a la ___
hints: Todo recto comes first; luego means 'then'. The turn that follows is to the left: a la izquierda.
activities.feedback: Izquierda is left. Derecha is the opposite, and a la is fixed in front of both of them.

segments.text: Complete the directions: Todo recto, luego a la

errors.explanation: Derecha is 'right'. The passerby said to turn left after going straight: a la izquierda.
Direction phrases use the fixed feminine form a la izquierda; izquierdo appears with masculine nouns (el lado izquierdo).

activities.prompt: Soften the question by putting Perdone in front: ¿Dónde está la estación?
hints: Perdone goes ahead of the question, comma after it — the question itself stays exactly as it was, with its accent on dónde.
activities.feedback: Perdone goes ahead of the question and a comma separates it. The accent on dónde stays, because it is still the word asking where.

errors.explanation: The polite opener Perdone must come first — strangers get that courtesy: Perdone, ¿dónde está la estación?
Perdona is the informal tú form. For a stranger use the formal Perdone.

activities.prompt: Spanish fences a question with two marks, the first of them upside down. Which of these is asking the price?
activities.feedback: ¿Cuánto cuesta? is the price question: cuánto asks how much, cuesta comes from costar, and both marks are obligatory.

activities.prompt: At a café in Seville you are pricing one coffee only. Ask the question.
activities.feedback: Cuesta is singular because one coffee is being priced; for several the verb would turn into cuestan.

activities.prompt: You think the price is fair. Turn «Es caro.» into its opposite.
activities.feedback: No goes before the verb es; Spanish never lets the negation wander to the end of the sentence.

activities.prompt: Dinner in Madrid is over and you want to settle up. Ask the waiter for the bill.
activities.feedback: Cuenta is feminine, so it takes la, and por favor is what keeps the request polite.

activities.body: Spanish weekdays are the Roman sky turned into a calendar: lunes is the moon, martes Mars, miércoles Mercury, jueves Jupiter and viernes Venus. Then the naming breaks — sábado comes from the Sabbath and domingo from the Lord’s day. The days are masculine and lower-case, and Spanish needs no separate word for ‘on’: the article el carries it, as in el lunes. Watch out, too: mañana is tomorrow, while la mañana is the morning.

activities.prompt: Your Madrid phone writes a label above the date. Tap the label for today.
hints: Hoy is the label for today. Mañana is tomorrow, lunes a weekday and semana the week — the phone's label for the current day is hoy.
activities.feedback: That is hoy. The decoys mean tomorrow, Monday and the week.

activities.prompt: Build the Spanish sentence for on Monday I work; the article carries the on.
hints: The article El carries the 'on' and sits first, then the day lunes, then the verb trabajo: El lunes trabajo.
activities.feedback: El sits in front of the day and means on: el lunes, on Monday.

activities.prompt: Complete the Spanish for on Mondays, meaning every Monday: ___ lunes trabajo.
hints: The plural article Los makes it 'on Mondays' — every Monday, a habit. El would mean one single Monday; the prompt says every Monday.
activities.feedback: Spanish uses the plural article for a repeated day: los lunes, on Mondays.

segments.text: Complete the Spanish for on Mondays, meaning every Monday:

errors.explanation: El lunes means one single Monday. 'On Mondays', every Monday, needs the plural: los lunes.
Lunes is masculine, so the plural article is los, never las.
La is feminine and singular; the repeated-day habit needs the masculine plural: los lunes.

activities.prompt: Predict the sentence before you write it: today is Friday.
hints: Dates and days ride ser, not estar: Hoy es … Then the day, lower-case as the intro taught: viernes.
activities.feedback: Hoy es plus the day. Viernes still carries the name of Venus.

errors.explanation: Days and dates ride ser, not estar — the day is what it is: Hoy es viernes.
The prompt asks for Friday — hoy es viernes. Martes is the day of Mars, not the answer.
The time word hoy leads in Spanish: Hoy es viernes.

activities.prompt: Give the English meaning: El lunes trabajo.
hints: El in front of a weekday carries the 'on' — there is no separate word for it. Read the article with the day, then the work: On Monday I work.
activities.feedback: There is no separate word for on here; the article el does that work in front of the day.

errors.explanation: The little 'on' is hiding in the article el — 'on Monday' is part of the sentence: On Monday I work.
Trabajo is the present 'I work'. The sentence is about a habit, not a finished past: On Monday I work.
The article el means 'on' here; English needs no extra article with the day: I work on Monday.

activities.prompt: Five Spanish weekdays carry the name of a planet or a god. Which pair leaves that company?
hints: The prompt asks which pair does NOT follow the sky names. Sábado came from the Sabbath and domingo from the Lord's day — those two broke away, so they are the odd pair out.
activities.feedback: Sábado comes from the Sabbath and domingo from the Lord's day; lunes to viernes are the old sky names.

activities.prompt: Read the week. Which day does the passage name after the moon?
hints: The passage's first line names the day: El lunes es el día de la Luna. Which weekday is the day of the moon?
activities.feedback: The first line says it: el lunes is the day of la Luna, the moon.

errors.explanation: Martes is the day the writer works — the moon day is lunes.
Viernes is the rest day; the moon gets lunes: El lunes es el día de la Luna.
The moon is what the day is NAMED after — the question asks for the day itself: lunes.

activities.prompt: One letter separates the Spanish words for brother and sister. Which of these four is the sister?
activities.feedback: Hermana is the sister; the -a ending marks her feminine, as -o marks hermano. Padres is the pair of parents, and la familia is the household.

activities.prompt: Hermana is feminine and keeps the same article as the subject. Choose the line that correctly says I have a sister.
activities.feedback: Una hermana keeps the feminine article una; un hermana and unos hermana are the two ways learners get this wrong.

activities.prompt: You are describing the one brother you have. Predict the form before you write it: I have a brother.
activities.feedback: Tener is irregular, so the I form is tengo and never tene: Tengo un hermano.

activities.prompt: Read what Ana wrote about her family. Which city are the parents still in?
activities.feedback: The brother and sister are in Seville and Valencia; the closing sentence keeps the parents in Madrid.

activities.prompt: Make the sentence talk about two sisters instead of one: Tengo una hermana.
activities.feedback: The plural adds -s to hermana, and una becomes dos: Tengo dos hermanas.

activities.body: You already know the polite café request from «At the café». Today you build it yourself, block by block. Every polite request in this lesson is made of the same blocks: the softened verb quisiera, the drink with un, and por favor at the end. Notice the order — the verb always opens, and por favor always closes.

activities.prompt: Build the polite request for one coffee, starting with the softened verb.
activities.feedback: Quisiera opens, un café names the drink, and por favor closes — that order never changes.

activities.prompt: Build the polite request for one tea.
activities.feedback: Same frame, new drink — and the accent on té stays.

activities.prompt: The verb is missing. Complete the polite request.
activities.feedback: Quisiera is the softened form of quiero — the polite opener.

activities.prompt: Which of these is the polite way to ask for coffee?
activities.feedback: Quisiera softens the verb, quiero is blunt, and word order matters.

activities.prompt: Build the short polite request — no verb, just the drink.
activities.feedback: Drop the verb and the request still works: Un café, por favor.

activities.prompt: Type the polite request for one tea.
activities.feedback: Quisiera un té, por favor. — the accent on té is part of the spelling.

activities.prompt: Fill the blank, and mind the accent — the drink is tea.
activities.feedback: Té keeps its accent. Without it, te means something else entirely.

activities.prompt: A friend joins you and wants tea too. Build the polite request for one tea — from memory.
activities.feedback: You built it without the frame in front of you. That is the point of today.

activities.body: A friend is waiting for you at a café across town, and your phone is dead. Your mission has four parts: ask where the café is, follow the directions you are given, order a coffee politely, and ask for the bill. Everything you need was taught in «Asking the way», «At the café», and «Prices and paying». Read the mission card, then go.

activities.prompt: You stop a passerby. Which question asks where the café is?
hints: Dónde asks 'where' and opens the question; your target is the café: ¿Dónde está el café? The price question ¿Cuánto cuesta? belongs to the bill, later in the mission.
activities.feedback: Dónde asks 'where' — and it keeps its accent because it is a question.

activities.prompt: Complete the question.
hints: The blank holds the asking word for 'where' — capital D, with the accent you learned in «Asking the way».
activities.feedback: Dónde with the accent asks 'where' — the directions lesson used it with the station, and it works for the café too.

errors.explanation: Qué means 'what' or 'that' — the place question wants the where-word: ¿Dónde está el café?
Cómo is 'how'. Asking where the café is needs dónde: ¿Dónde está el café?

activities.prompt: The passerby says: «A la izquierda, luego todo recto.» What do you do first?
hints: Luego means 'then'. The direction first on the list is the one you do first: turn left, then go straight ahead.
activities.feedback: A la izquierda is 'to the left', and luego tells you the straight part comes second.

options.text: Turn left, then go straight ahead.
Turn right, then go straight ahead.
Go straight ahead, then turn left.

activities.prompt: The next turn is to the right. Complete the direction.
hints: The next turn is to the right — 'to the right' is a la derecha, the twin of a la izquierda.
activities.feedback: A la derecha — right. The directions lesson paired it against a la izquierda.

errors.explanation: Izquierda is 'left' — the turn you already took. This one is to the right: derecha.
The fixed direction phrase is a la derecha, with the feminine form; derecho is the masculine word used with nouns (el lado derecho).

activities.prompt: You found the café. Order one coffee, politely.
hints: The polite order goes Quisiera + un + café, and por favor closes it — the same frame you practiced at the café.
activities.feedback: Quisiera wins again. But the server shakes her head — the coffee is finished!

activities.prompt: No coffee left. What do you order instead?
hints: Keep the exact polite frame and swap the drink: tea is té — Quisiera un té, por favor.
activities.feedback: Tea saves the mission — same polite frame, and the accent on té stays.

activities.prompt: Mission nearly complete. Ask for the bill, the way «Prices and paying» taught you.
hints: The bill request from «Prices and paying»: two words plus por favor — La cuenta, por favor.
activities.feedback: La cuenta, por favor. — mission complete: you found the café, ordered politely, and paid.

errors.explanation: The polite line keeps por favor: La cuenta, por favor.
La belongs with cuenta — the bill is la cuenta: La cuenta, por favor.
Por favor is two separate words.

activities.body: No new words today — this lesson is pure memory. Every answer comes from a lesson you have already finished: «First words», «Introducing yourself», «Days and times», and «Family and people». Each prompt names the lesson where you first met the answer. If you hesitate, think back to that lesson before you guess.

activities.prompt: You learned this in «First words». How do you say 'thank you'?
activities.feedback: Gracias — one of your very first Spanish words, and still the most useful.

activities.prompt: You learned this in «Introducing yourself». Complete the sentence.
activities.feedback: Me llamo — literally 'I call myself', the way Spanish introduces a name.

activities.prompt: You learned this in «Introducing yourself». Someone asks «¿Cómo te llamas?» — answer that your name is Ana.
activities.feedback: Me llamo Ana. — the full introduction, rebuilt from memory.

activities.prompt: You learned this in «Days and times». Which word means 'tomorrow'?
activities.feedback: Mañana — and mind the ñ, it is not a plain n.

activities.prompt: You learned this in «Family and people». Complete the phrase — it means 'the parents'.
activities.feedback: Los padres — los for the plural, the way «Family and people» taught it.

activities.prompt: You learned this in «Introducing yourself». Put the words in order to ask someone's name.
activities.feedback: ¿Cómo te llamas? — exactly as the lesson taught it.

activities.prompt: You learned this in «Introducing yourself». Which of these means 'nice to meet you'?
activities.feedback: Mucho gusto — literally 'much pleasure', the standard reply after an introduction.

activities.prompt: You learned this in «First words». Say 'yes, thank you'.
activities.feedback: Sí, gracias. — two of your very first Spanish words, still together.

activities.prompt: Last one, from «Family and people». Which means 'the sister'?
activities.feedback: La hermana — la for feminine, hermana for sister. Four lessons revisited, nothing new added.

activities.body: You are in Madrid and the museum closes at six. Your phone is dead, so your Spanish has to do the work. Your mission has four parts: ask a passerby where the museum is, follow the directions you are given, ask the price of a ticket, and thank the cashier. Everything you need was taught in «Asking the way» and «Prices and paying». Read the mission card, then go.

activities.prompt: You stop a passerby. Which question asks where the museum is?
hints: Dónde opens a where-question and el museo names the target. ¿Cuánto cuesta? asks the price — you will need it at the ticket desk, not on the street.
activities.feedback: ¿Dónde? opens a where-question and el museo names your target. ¿Cuánto cuesta? asks the price — useful later, not now.

activities.prompt: Complete the question. Notice the accent — it is the same word you learned in «Asking the way».
hints: The blank holds the asking word that means 'where' — the same accent-carrying word from «Asking the way» and the earlier mission steps.
activities.feedback: Dónde with the accent means 'where'. Without it, donde is a different, plain word — the accent carries the meaning.

errors.explanation: Qué is 'what' — the place question needs the where-word: ¿Dónde está el museo?
Cómo is 'how'. Asking where the museum is takes dónde: ¿Dónde está el museo?

activities.prompt: The passerby says: «A la derecha, luego todo recto.» What do you do first?
hints: Derecha is 'right', and it comes before luego ('then') — you turn right first, then go straight ahead.
activities.feedback: A la derecha comes first — you turn right, and only luego, afterwards, do you go todo recto. Order matters in directions.

options.text: Go back the way you came

activities.prompt: You took a wrong turn. A shopkeeper points and says the museum is on the left. Complete the direction you hear.
hints: The shopkeeper points left — 'to the left' is a la izquierda, the twin of the derecha you just followed.
activities.feedback: A la izquierda — left. Keep it next to its twin a la derecha and you can follow almost any direction in Spain.

errors.explanation: Derecha is 'right' — the museum is on the left, so the word is izquierda.
Direction phrases use the fixed feminine form a la izquierda; izquierdo pairs with masculine nouns (el lado izquierdo).

activities.prompt: You reach the ticket desk. Which question asks the price of a ticket?
hints: Price questions use ¿Cuánto cuesta? — 'how much does it cost?' — the phrase from «Prices and paying». La cuenta belongs to a café table, not a ticket desk.
activities.feedback: ¿Cuánto cuesta? asks 'how much does it cost?' — you learned it in «Prices and paying». La cuenta is the bill at a café, not a ticket desk.

activities.prompt: The cashier answers «Son diez euros.» and hands you the ticket. What do you say?
hints: The ticket is in your hand — that is the moment for gracias. Hola was for arriving; mucho gusto is for meeting someone new.
activities.feedback: Gracias thanks — exactly the moment it was made for. Hola greets on arrival; mucho gusto is for meeting people, not tickets.

activities.prompt: Say the question to yourself, then type it: ask where the museum is.
hints: The question from step 2, straight from memory: ¿Dónde está el museo? — same words, same order, same accent.
activities.feedback: ¿Dónde está el museo? — the same question that started your mission. Notice how much faster it comes now.

errors.explanation: The article el sits between the verb and the museum: ¿Dónde está el museo?
Position takes estar, not ser: ¿Dónde está el museo?
Museo is masculine — its article is el, not la: ¿Dónde está el museo?

activities.prompt: Mission complete — you are inside the museum. You spot a friend across the hall: greet them, and thank the passerby who helped you. Type both.
hints: Two one-word lines: Hola. for your friend across the hall, Gracias. for the passerby who pointed you here.
activities.feedback: Hola greets, Gracias thanks — the two smallest words in your Spanish, and the two you will use most.

errors.explanation: Both parts of the mission close matter — the thank-you is missing: Hola. Gracias.
The greeting is missing: greet your friend first, then thank — Hola. Gracias.
Adiós is goodbye — you are greeting your friend, so open with Hola: Hola. Gracias.

activities.body: Your friend has invited you to a birthday party, and your brother and sister are coming too. Your mission has five parts: greet the host, introduce yourself, ask two guests their names, introduce your brother and your sister, and answer mucho gusto like you mean it. Everything you need was taught in «Introducing yourself» and «Family and people». Read the mission card, then walk in.

activities.prompt: You arrive at the door. Which word greets the host?
hints: You have just arrived — the universal opener is hola; adiós is what you say when you leave.
activities.feedback: Hola opens every Spanish conversation — say it the moment you arrive, not when you leave. That is what adiós is for.

activities.prompt: The host asks your name. Build the answer: 'My name is Leo.'
hints: The answer opens with the pronoun Me, then the verb llamo, then your name: Me llamo Leo.
activities.feedback: Me llamo Leo — literally 'I call myself Leo'. The me points back at you; that little pronoun is doing the real work.

activities.prompt: Now you want to know the guest's name. Which question do you ask?
hints: Flip the pronoun: me is for yourself (Me llamo), te points at the other person — ¿Cómo te llamas?
activities.feedback: ¿Cómo te llamas? — me llamo says my name, te llamas asks yours. Never swap me and te.

activities.prompt: The guest answers, and you reply politely. Complete the phrase.
hints: The fixed closer that means 'much pleasure' — the missing noun is gusto.
activities.feedback: Mucho gusto — 'much pleasure'. It is the handshake of Spanish small talk; use it with every new name.

errors.explanation: Mucho gracias is not a phrase — the reply to a new name is mucho gusto ('much pleasure').
The fixed phrase uses the noun gusto ('pleasure'); gusta is a verb form — the closer is Mucho gusto.

activities.prompt: Your sister Ana arrives. Introduce her — build: 'The sister is Ana.'
hints: Start with the feminine article La, then hermana, then es, then her name: La hermana es Ana.
activities.feedback: La hermana es Ana — la because hermana is feminine. The article and the noun always travel together and always agree.

activities.prompt: Which sentence correctly says the brother is Leo?
hints: Hermano is masculine, so its article must agree: El hermano es Leo. La would need a sister, los a plural.
activities.feedback: El hermano — masculine article with a masculine noun. La hermana would need a sister, and los needs a plural.

activities.prompt: Complete the sentence about your brother.
hints: The blank holds the masculine singular article that agrees with hermano — one brother, so not los.
activities.feedback: El hermano — el marks masculine singular. Say the pair together until el hermano feels like one word.

errors.explanation: La goes with feminine nouns (la hermana). Hermano is masculine — the article is El.
Los is plural ('the brothers'). One brother takes the singular article: El hermano.

activities.prompt: A new guest joins the party. Type the polite reply you give after hearing their name.
hints: The two-word closer from step 5, typed from memory: Mucho gusto.
activities.feedback: Mucho gusto. — two words, and you already own them.

errors.explanation: The phrase uses the noun gusto — gusta is a verb form. Say Mucho gusto.
Gracias thanks someone; the closer for a new name is mucho gusto.

activities.prompt: Mission complete — the party is in full swing. One last guest arrives and asks your name. Introduce yourself from memory.
hints: Either form you practiced works from memory: Me llamo Leo. or Soy Leo. — the pronoun version is the one this mission built.
activities.feedback: Me llamo Leo or Soy Leo — either opens the door. Notice which one your mouth reaches for first; that is the one you truly know.

errors.explanation: The reflexive verb needs its pronoun me — without it, the verb belongs to nobody: Me llamo Leo.
Llamo is the I-form; llama means he/she says. Talking about yourself, use Me llamo Leo.

activities.body: Spanish family sentences are small machines: a name or soy / me llamo up front, es to link the person, and an article that must match — el with hermano, la with hermana. You already know every part from «Introducing yourself» and «Family and people». This lesson just bolts them together. Notice the patterns in the examples, then build.

activities.prompt: Build the introduction: 'My name is Ana.'
activities.feedback: Me llamo Ana — me, then llamo, then the name. That order never changes.

activities.prompt: Now build: 'I am the brother.'
activities.feedback: Soy el hermano — soy first, then the article-noun pair. El hermano travels as a unit.

activities.prompt: The noun is missing. Complete the sentence about the sister.
activities.feedback: La hermana — la told you the noun was feminine before you even read it. Articles are clues, not decoration.

activities.prompt: Which article belongs with 'hermano'?
activities.feedback: El hermano — masculine singular takes el. Los is plural, la is feminine, and una is the wrong job entirely.

activities.prompt: Build the full sentence: 'The brother is Leo.'
activities.feedback: El hermano es Leo — subject first, es in the middle, the name last. Spanish links with es the way English links with 'is'.

activities.prompt: Type the introduction from memory: 'My name is Ana.'
activities.feedback: Me llamo Ana. — from tiles to typing; the sentence is yours now.

activities.prompt: The article is missing. Complete the sentence.
activities.feedback: Soy el hermano — even after soy, the article stays. Spanish never drops it the way English drops 'the' in 'I am brother'.

activities.prompt: Which sentence is correct?
activities.feedback: El hermano es Leo — every article agrees with its noun. In the wrong answers the article and the noun disagree, and Spanish ears catch it instantly.

activities.prompt: From memory: build 'Ana is the sister.'
activities.feedback: Ana es la hermana — name, es, article, noun. Four pieces, one pattern, and it works for your whole family.

activities.body: A Spanish noun never travels alone: it carries its article, and the article tells you the gender — el for masculine, la for feminine. In the plural they become los and las. And when the little words a and de meet el, they fuse: a + el is always al, de + el is always del.

activities.prompt: Cocina is feminine. Which article belongs with it?
hints: Cocina ends in -a and the moving-day tour introduced it as la cocina — the feminine singular article. El is masculine, and los/las are plural, so only la fits.
activities.feedback: Cocina is feminine and singular, so it takes la. El is masculine, and los and las are plural.

activities.prompt: Predict the sentence before you write it: the table is in the kitchen.
hints: Build it from left to right: mesa is feminine like cocina (la mesa), a location takes está (not es), and en means in — La mesa está en la cocina.
activities.feedback: Mesa is feminine, so la mesa; está places it, and en means in: La mesa está en la cocina.

answers: La mesa está en la cocina.

errors.answer: La mesa es en la cocina.
errors.explanation: Es says what a thing is; being in a place takes está: La mesa está en la cocina.
The room carries its article — en la cocina, not en cocina.

errors.answer: El mesa está en la cocina.
errors.explanation: Mesa is feminine, so la mesa — exactly like la cocina in the story.

activities.prompt: The contraction al is a + el fused. Choose the correct line for I'm going to the bathroom.
hints: The lesson's rule: a + el always fuses into al. Reject the option that splits them (a el), the one that reverses the trip (del = from the bathroom), and the gender mismatch (la baño) — only al survives.
activities.feedback: A + el always fuses into al — a el is never written. Del would mean from the bathroom, the opposite trip.

activities.prompt: Translate into Spanish: I come from the living room.
hints: Vengo is 'I come', and the little word de meets el and fuses — the story's evening walk used the same contraction: Vengo del salón.
activities.feedback: Vengo is I come, and de + el fuses: Vengo del salón.

errors.explanation: De + el never stay separate — they fuse into the single word del: Vengo del salón.
The fused de + el (del) belongs in the phrase: Vengo del salón.
Baño is the bathroom — the step asks for the living room, salón: Vengo del salón.

activities.prompt: Dormitorio is masculine. Fill the gap: ___ dormitorio es pequeño.
hints: The prompt already hands you the gender: dormitorio is masculine, and es pequeño is singular — that leaves the masculine singular article El.
activities.feedback: Dormitorio is masculine, so it takes el: El dormitorio es pequeño.

segments.text: Dormitorio is masculine. Fill the gap:

errors.explanation: Dormitorio is masculine, so it takes el, not la.
Es pequeño is singular, so the article is singular too: el, not los.
Las is the feminine plural; dormitorio is masculine and singular — El.

activities.body: Spanish plurals follow one friendly rule: a word ending in a vowel simply adds -s — libros, mesas. A word ending in a consonant adds -es — flores, ciudades — and lápiz politely changes its z to a c: lápices. Don't forget the article: el becomes los and la becomes las.

activities.body: Regular -ar verbs are a small machine: remove -ar, then add -o for I and -a for he or she. Trabajo, trabaja; estudio, estudia. To say when, Spanish uses por with the part of day: por la mañana, por la tarde, por la noche — always por, never en.

activities.body: Saying no in Spanish is beautifully simple: put no right in front of the verb — no trabajo, no estudia. activities.body: Comer and beber follow the regular -er pattern: como, comes, come and bebo, bebes, bebe. Then comes Spanish's famous backwards verb: me gusta. activities.body: Ir is the verb for going, and it's irregular in a friendly way: voy, vas, va, vamos, van. Getting there is just as easy: en plus the vehicle — en coche, en metro, en autobús. The one exception is your own two feet: a pie, on foot. And the destination follows a: Voy al centro.

activities.body: The past tense in Spanish is refreshingly regular to start: -ar verbs take -é for I — hablé, trabajé, estudié — and -er/-ir verbs take -í — comí, viví. Then memorise one small giant: fue, which means both was and went. Set the scene with ayer or anoche, and you're telling stories.
