segments.text: You want a bottle. Fill the gap: Una

errors.explanation: The Spanish word for bottle is botella: Una botella de agua, por favor.
Bolsa is a bag — the market container for water is una botella.

activities.body: Spanish pain is backwards, just like Spanish liking: Me duele la cabeza — literally, the head hurts to me. One aching part takes duele; several take duelen: Me duelen las manos. And body parts wear the article, not a possessive: la cabeza, las manos. When it's serious: Voy al médico.

activities.prompt: Which line says my head hurts?
hints: Pain runs backwards like liking: me + duele — the head hurts to me. The other lines use the wrong reflexive (me duelo), a possessive (mi cabeza), or scramble the order (Duele me).
activities.feedback: Doler works like gustar — duele agrees with la cabeza — and body parts take the article: Me duele la cabeza.

activities.prompt: Predict the sentence before you write it: my hands hurt.
hints: Las manos is plural, so the backwards verb stretches into duelen — the story's noon line used the same switch: Me duelen las manos.
activities.feedback: Las manos is plural, so doler becomes duelen: Me duelen las manos.

errors.explanation: Las manos is plural, so the verb agrees and becomes duelen: Me duelen las manos.
Manos is feminine, so its plural article is las: las manos.
Me duelo would be 'I hurt myself' — the hands hurt, so duele's plural: duelen.

activities.prompt: The noun is singular. Choose the verb that matches: Me ___ el estómago.
hints: El estómago is singular, so the backwards verb stays duele — the form the clinic scene used; duelen would need several body parts, and me duelo is the reflexive slip.
activities.feedback: El estómago is singular, so duele stays singular: Me duele el estómago.

activities.prompt: Translate into Spanish: I have a fever.
hints: Spanish carries a fever with tener, it doesn't be it — your form is tengo, and the fever rides bare: Tengo fiebre.
activities.feedback: Spanish has a fever rather than being feverish: Tengo fiebre.

errors.explanation: A fever is carried with tener, not estar: Tengo fiebre.
Fiebre here is a general condition and takes no article: Tengo fiebre.
The infinitive needs its ending — your I form is tengo: Tengo fiebre.

activities.prompt: Body parts take the article, not a possessive. Fill the gap: Me duele ___.
hints: The prompt states the rule: the article, not a possessive. The part that woke Pablo up wrong was la cabeza — Me duele la cabeza.
activities.feedback: The article, not a possessive, with body parts: Me duele la cabeza.

segments.text: Body parts take the article, not a possessive. Fill the gap: Me duele

errors.explanation: Spanish uses the article, not a possessive, with body parts: la cabeza.
Cabeza is feminine — the article is la: la cabeza.
The body part keeps its article: la cabeza.

activities.prompt: Which line correctly asks for something for a headache?
hints: Ask with Tiene (the formal you), then algo, then para for 'for', then el dolor de cabeza. The traps swap para for por or drop the article.
activities.feedback: Para marks purpose, and de cabeza completes the phrase: ¿Tiene algo para el dolor de cabeza?

options.text: ¿Tiene algo para el dolor de cabeza?
¿Tiene algo por el dolor de cabeza?
¿Necesito algo para el dolor de cabeza?

activities.prompt: Predict the sentence before you write it: I need these pills.
hints: State the need in one line: Necesito + the feminine plural pointer estas + pastillas.
activities.feedback: Necesito plus the noun: Necesito estas pastillas.

errors.explanation: Pastillas is plural, so the pointer must agree: estas pastillas.
Pastillas is feminine — the plural pointer is estas, not estos.
The pointer estas ('these') points at the pills you need: Necesito estas pastillas.

activities.prompt: Purpose takes para. Choose the correct line.
hints: Only the purpose word decides this one: para marks 'for the purpose of' — not por, not de, not a.
activities.feedback: Para means for the purpose of: Algo para la fiebre, por favor.

options.text: Algo para la fiebre, por favor.
Algo por la fiebre, por favor.
Algo de la fiebre, por favor.
Algo a la fiebre, por favor.

activities.prompt: Put the words in order: do you have something for the pain? (formal)
hints: Open with ¿Tiene, then algo, then the purpose linker para, then el dolor.
activities.feedback: ¿Tiene algo para el dolor? — tiene for the formal you, para for purpose.

activities.prompt: Translate into Spanish: I need a prescription.
hints: Necesito + una + receta — receta is feminine, so the article is una.
activities.feedback: Necesito plus the noun: Necesito una receta.

errors.explanation: Receta is feminine — it takes una, not un: Necesito una receta.
The article una belongs in front of receta: Necesito una receta.

activities.prompt: The pharmacy is close by. Fill the gap: La farmacia está ___.
hints: 'The pharmacy is ___' — the gap word means 'nearby'; you are almost there.
activities.feedback: Cerca means nearby: La farmacia está cerca.

segments.text: The pharmacy is close by. Fill the gap: La farmacia está

errors.explanation: Lejos means 'far' — the pharmacy is close by, which is cerca.
Cercano is an adjective that describes a noun; after está you need the adverb cerca ('nearby').

activities.body: Emergencies run on short, strong phrases: ¡Socorro! and Necesito ayuda. The command to call for help uses the formal form — ¡Llame a una ambulancia! — because emergencies are no place for casual speech. And the number to know across all of Europe is 112.

activities.prompt: Which line gives the formal command to call an ambulance?
hints: Emergencies use the formal command: Llame with -e. Llama is the tú form, Llame una drops the needed a, and Llamar is the bare infinitive.
activities.feedback: Llame is the formal command, and llamar needs its a: Llame a una ambulancia.

activities.prompt: Predict the question before you write it: where is the hospital?
hints: Dónde takes its accent, está says where something is, and the hospital needs its article: ¿Dónde está el hospital?
activities.feedback: Dónde with its accent, está for location: ¿Dónde está el hospital?

errors.explanation: Location takes estar, not ser: ¿Dónde está el hospital?
The hospital needs its article el: ¿Dónde está el hospital?
Dónde carries its accent when it asks where: ¿Dónde está el hospital?

activities.prompt: Emergencies use the formal command. Choose the correct cry.
hints: The formal command is Llame — the usted form. Llamo means 'I call' (useless when asking for help), and Llamar/Llames are the wrong shape for a command.
activities.feedback: Llame is the usted command — Llamo would mean I call, which helps nobody.

activities.prompt: Put the words in order: call an ambulance, please.
hints: The formal command Llame leads, then a + una + ambulancia, then por favor to soften it: Llame a una ambulancia, por favor.
activities.feedback: The command first, then a una ambulancia: Llame a una ambulancia, por favor.

activities.prompt: Translate into Spanish: I need help!
hints: Necesito + ayuda — no article in between — and the exclamation marks frame the cry: ¡Necesito ayuda!
activities.feedback: Necesito ayuda, with the marks that frame it: ¡Necesito ayuda!

errors.explanation: Ayudas is 'you help'; the noun is ayuda: ¡Necesito ayuda!
The cry carries no article: Necesito ayuda. La ayuda would mean a specific help.
Ayuda is feminine and takes no article in this cry: Necesito ayuda.

activities.prompt: This is the cry for help. Fill the gap: ¡___!
hints: This is the standalone shout for help — the intro's very first phrase: ¡Socorro!
activities.feedback: ¡Socorro! is the cry for help.

segments.text: This is the cry for help. Fill the gap: ¡

errors.explanation: ¡Ayuda! is the other cry of the lesson, but the taught shout for help is ¡Socorro!.
Llame starts the command 'Llame a una ambulancia'; the bare cry for help is ¡Socorro!.
Emergencia names the situation, not the cry. The shout is ¡Socorro!.

activities.prompt: Read the emergency. What does the woman call?
hints: The passage names her action: Una mujer llama a una ambulancia. The man shouts ¡Socorro! — the woman calls the ambulance.
activities.feedback: The second sentence says it: llama a una ambulancia.

errors.explanation: No police here — the woman calls a una ambulancia.
Socorro is the man's shout; the woman calls an ambulance.
112 is the number to know, but the passage says the woman calls a una ambulancia.

activities.prompt: Which line accepts the invitation?
activities.feedback: ¡Claro que sí! is the warm yes; Lo siento, no puedo is the gentle no.

activities.prompt: Predict the question before you write it: do you want to come? (informal)
activities.feedback: Querer takes -es for you: ¿Quieres venir?

activities.prompt: Invitar needs its a. Choose the correct invitation.
activities.feedback: The a bridges invito to the place: Te invito a mi casa.

activities.prompt: Translate into Spanish: I'm sorry, I can't.
activities.feedback: The gentle decline: Lo siento, no puedo.

activities.prompt: Read the invitation. Does Pablo accept?
activities.feedback: His answer is the warm yes: ¡Claro que sí, gracias!

activities.body: The past in Spanish is a habit, not a rule to memorize. For things that are done and dusted, -ar verbs take -é, -aste, -ó, -amos, -aron (hablé, hablaste, habló) and -er/-ir verbs take -í, -iste, -ió, -imos, -ieron (comí, comiste, comió). Then there are the rebels you will use every day — tuve, hice, dije, estuvo — no pattern, just friends you memorize by meeting them.

activities.prompt: Which ending marks the yo form of -ar verbs in the past?
hints: The yo past of -ar verbs ends in -é: trabajé. Trabajo is present, trabaja another person's present, trabajar the infinitive — only trabajé is the done-and-dusted I-form.
activities.feedback: trabajé — the é is the I-did-it marker. trabajo is present (I work), trabaja is he/she present, trabajar is the untouched infinitive.

activities.prompt: Predict the yo past of comer: Yesterday I ate → Ayer ___ .
hints: Comer is an -er verb, so the yo past ends in -í: comí. The accent is part of the spelling.
activities.feedback: -er/-ir verbs take -í for yo: comí. Keep the accent — comi without it is a spelling mistake, not a past tense.

errors.explanation: The yo past carries its accent: comí.
Como is the present 'I eat'; yesterday needs the past comí.
Comer is the infinitive; the sentence needs the conjugated past form comí.

activities.prompt: Estuvo enfermo ayer. Which verb is the rebel here?
hints: Estuvo is estar's past — it ignores the -ar pattern completely, so it is the rebel. Enfermo is an adjective, ayer a time word, and fue is not even in the sentence.
activities.feedback: estuvo — estar's past ignores the -ar pattern completely (no *estó). enfermo is an adjective, ayer a time word, and fue isn't even in the sentence.

activities.prompt: Put the words in order: We ate paella on Sunday.
hints: Verb first, then what, then when: Comimos paella el domingo. The past verb Comimos leads the whole sentence.
activities.feedback: Comimos paella el domingo — verb first, then what, then when. The past verb carries the whole sentence.

activities.prompt: Translate into Spanish: He told me no.
hints: Decir's past is dijo ('he told'), and the que links the telling to the 'no': Me dijo que no. Me dije would be 'I told myself'.
activities.feedback: decir → dijo in the past — one of the rebels. Me dijo que no: told-me that no.

errors.explanation: The told-me-that-no bridge needs que: Me dijo que no.
Dije is 'I said'; the prompt says 'he told me' — Me dijo que no.
Decía is the habit-tense; a single 'he told me' takes dijo: Me dijo que no.

activities.prompt: Anoche ___ la tarea. (hacer, yo)
hints: Hacer's yo past is the rebel hice — no pattern, just a friend to memorize: Anoche hice la tarea.
activities.feedback: hacer → hice. The yo past of hacer drops the pattern — memorize hice the way you memorized fue.

errors.explanation: Hago is the present 'I do'; anoche calls the past hice.
Hizo is 'he/she did'; the prompt says yo — hice.
Hacía is the habit-tense; a done-and-dusted task takes hice.

activities.prompt: Read the day. What time did the narrator get home?
hints: The story's last sentence gives it: llegué a casa a las once. The time is a las once — not the seven o'clock of getting up.
activities.feedback: Llegué a casa a las once — the last pretérito of the story, and your answer.

errors.explanation: Seven was when the narrator got UP; home came at a las once.
Friends were the dinner company; the question asks the time he got home — a las once.
The report was finished in the afternoon; getting home happened a las once.

activities.body: Before rules, feel the difference: Habló = he spoke, done. Hablaba = he was speaking, ongoing. The imperfecto is the movie camera — era, iba, jugaba paint the scene while the action happens. The forms are kind: -ar verbs take -aba (hablaba), -er/-ir verbs take -ía (comía, vivía), and there are only three rebels in the whole tense: era, iba, veía.

activities.prompt: Which sentence describes a habit in the past?
hints: The album's first caption is the model: de niño jugaba = 'used to play', the stretched habit. Ayer jugué snaps it shut (pretérito), and the present forms (juego, mañana juego) are the wrong time.
activities.feedback: jugaba = used to play, the habit. jugué = played once and done; juego = present. Only the imperfecto stretches time into a habit.

activities.prompt: Predict the imperfecto of ser (he/she was, setting the scene).
hints: Ser is one of the three irregular imperfectos the intro named — era, iba, veía. Era paints the scene; the pretérito fue would snap it shut.
activities.feedback: era — one of only three irregular imperfectos (era, iba, veía). Everything else follows -aba/-ía.

errors.explanation: Fue is the pretérito — snapped shut. The imperfecto stretches the scene: era.
Es is the present; the scene-setting past of ser is era.

activities.prompt: Which is NOT a regular imperfecto form?
hints: The movie camera wears -aba and -ía — scan the endings: hablaba, comía and vivía all fit the pattern, while habló carries -ó, the pretérito's snapping ending. It is the odd one out.
activities.feedback: habló is pretérito — the -ó ending snaps the action shut. The -aba/-ía endings are the imperfecto's signature.

activities.prompt: Translate into Spanish: There were many people in the square.
hints: The frozen photo used había — the imperfecto of hay — and it stays singular even for many people: Había mucha gente en la plaza.
activities.feedback: había — the imperfecto of hay, for there-was scenes. No plural form: había covers many people too.

answers: Había mucha gente en la plaza.

errors.answer: Hay mucha gente en la plaza.
errors.explanation: Hay is the present; the past scene takes había.

errors.answer: Hubo mucha gente en la plaza.
errors.explanation: Hubo is the pretérito — a finished moment. The background scene takes había.

errors.answer: Había mucha gente en el plaza.
errors.explanation: Plaza is feminine: la plaza.

activities.prompt: De niño, ___ al fútbol todos los días. (jugar, yo)
hints: De niño + todos los días spells habit, and the prompt conjugates it for yo: jugar → jugaba — the very form that opened the album.
activities.feedback: De niño + todos los días = habit → imperfecto: jugaba. The time words decide the tense.

errors.explanation: Jugué is the pretérito — a finished game. 'Every day' needs the stretched habit: jugaba.
Juego is the present; the habit lives in the past: jugaba.
Jugo means 'juice' — the imperfecto is jugaba, keeping the -aba the camera uses.

activities.body: The future is the kindest tense in Spanish: don't touch the infinitive, just add endings — hablaré, comeré, viviré. One pattern for all three verb groups: -é, -ás, -á, -emos, -án. Then learn the six rebels that change their stem — tendré, podré, haré, diré, vendré, saldré — and you own tomorrow.

activities.prompt: How is the simple future formed?
hints: The future touches nothing: infinitive + endings. Hablar + é = hablaré — no stem change and nothing removed. -aba is the imperfecto, not the future.
activities.feedback: infinitive + endings: hablar + é = hablaré. -aba is the imperfecto; the infinitive stays whole — nothing is removed.

activities.prompt: Predict the yo future of comer.
hints: comer + é = comeré. The future uses the same endings for every verb group — comer keeps its full infinitive.
activities.feedback: comer + é = comeré. Same ending for -ar, -er and -ir — the future doesn't care about verb groups.

errors.explanation: The yo future carries its accent: comeré.
Comía is the imperfect habit-tense; the future of comer is comeré.
Comer is the infinitive; the future yo form keeps it and adds -é: comeré.

activities.prompt: Which verb keeps a normal stem in the future?
hints: Hablar keeps its stem — hablaré is the regular one. Tendré, podré and diré all trade in new stems; only hablaré follows the pattern.
activities.feedback: hablaré — hablar is regular. tener→tendré, poder→podré and decir→diré are three of the six rebel stems.

activities.prompt: Put the words in order: Tomorrow I will speak with him.
hints: When comes first — Mañana — then the future verb hablaré, then with whom: con él. Mañana hablaré con él.
activities.feedback: Mañana hablaré con él — when, what, with whom. The future verb carries the promise.

activities.prompt: Translate into Spanish: We will eat at two.
hints: comer + emos = comeremos ('we will eat'), then the time with its las: a las dos. The nosotros ending stresses its own first syllable.
activities.feedback: comer + emos = comeremos. The nosotros ending is the only one with the stress on the ending's first syllable.

errors.explanation: Comemos is the present 'we eat'; the plan wears the future: Comeremos a las dos.
The clock time needs its las — 'at two' is a las dos.
Comeré is 'I will eat'; the prompt says 'we' — Comeremos a las dos.

activities.prompt: El viernes ___ a cenar. (salir, nosotros)
hints: Salir is one of the six rebels: the stem becomes saldr-, and nosotros ends in -emos: saldremos.
activities.feedback: salir → saldr-: saldremos. The d sneaks in — one of the six rebels.

errors.explanation: Salimos is the present 'we leave'; the week ahead needs the future saldremos.
Saldrá is 'he/she will leave'; the prompt says nosotros — saldremos.
Regular future would be saliremos, but salir is a rebel: its stem is saldr-, so saldremos.

activities.prompt: Read the week ahead. When will the narrator travel to Barcelona?
hints: The first lines map the week: el lunes tendré una reunión, el martes viajaré a Barcelona. The Barcelona trip wears martes, not the meeting's lunes.
activities.feedback: el martes viajaré — the future verb plus its day. Plans wear dates.

errors.explanation: Monday holds the meeting; the trip to Barcelona is on martes.
Wednesday holds the presentation; Barcelona is on martes.
Friday is the celebration dinner; the Barcelona trip is on martes.

activities.body: The future isn't just tomorrow — it does three jobs. It promises: Te llamaré esta noche. It predicts: Mañana lloverá. And it wonders about right now: ¿Dónde estará? — where can he be? Watch for creo que, probablemente, seguro and quizá — they turn plain statements into forecasts.

activities.prompt: ¿Dónde estará? — What is the future doing here?
hints: The fortune teller isn't forecasting tomorrow here — estará wonders where he is right now. The intro named it the future's third job: a guess about the present.
activities.feedback: guessing about now — estará wonders where he is at this moment. The future of supposition isn't about tomorrow at all.

activities.prompt: Predict: there will be sun → ___ sol.
hints: Haber's future stem is habr-, and the -á ending makes 'there will be': habrá. The intro's examples — habrá gente, habrá tiempo — all use this one form.
activities.feedback: haber → habrá — the future of there-is. Habrá sol, habrá gente, habrá tiempo.

errors.explanation: Hay is the present 'there is'; the prediction needs the future habrá.
Habría is the conditional ('there would be'); for 'there will be' the future is habrá.
The future form carries its accent: habrá.

activities.prompt: Te llamaré esta noche is a…
hints: Te llamaré commits the speaker to actually calling — the future's promising job, the fortune teller's very first line. Predictions forecast weather; guesses wonder about now; habits live in the past.
activities.feedback: promise — te llamaré commits the speaker. Predictions need a forecast (lloverá); guesses wonder (estará).

activities.prompt: Translate into Spanish: I think it will rain tomorrow.
hints: Open with the booster creo que, pull the weather verb into the future — lloverá, with its accent — and drop mañana: Creo que lloverá mañana (or Creo que mañana lloverá).
activities.feedback: Creo que turns lloverá into a personal forecast. Prediction + booster = natural Spanish.

errors.explanation: Llueve is the present; the forecast needs the future lloverá.
The infinitive llover needs its future ending: lloverá.
The future form carries its accent: lloverá.

activities.prompt: ___ que vendrá. (I think…)
hints: The prompt hands you the meaning — 'I think' — and the que after the blank is already written. The lesson's booster is creo: Creo que vendrá.
activities.feedback: Creo que vendrá — I think he will come. The booster softens the prediction into an opinion.

errors.explanation: Cree is 'he/she thinks'; 'I think' is creo: Creo que vendrá.
The que in the sentence is already written — the blank holds just Creo: Creo que vendrá.
Pienso que is grammatical Spanish, but this lesson models the booster creo: Creo que vendrá.

activities.body: Decided plans don't wear the future tense — they wear ir a: Voy a estudiar medicina, vamos a comprar una casa. The decision is made; the ticket is bought. Add querer for the wish behind the plan: Quiero aprender italiano. Plan first with ir a, wish second with querer.

activities.prompt: Which sentence states a decided plan?
hints: Ir a carries a decided plan: Voy a estudiar medicina. Quizá is a maybe, estudiaba a past habit, estudié a finished past — none is a live plan.
activities.feedback: Voy a = decided and happening. quizá = maybe; estudiaba = used to; estudié = finished. Only ir a carries a live plan.

activities.prompt: Predict: you (tú) are going to come → ___ a venir.
hints: Ir hands tú the form vas; the a is the bridge and the second verb stays untouched: vas a venir.
activities.feedback: ir gives vas for tú — vas a venir. The a is the bridge; the second verb never changes.

errors.explanation: Voy is 'I am going'; the prompt says you (tú) — vas.
Va is he/she; you-tú is vas a venir.
Vamos is 'we'; the prompt asks for tú — vas.

activities.prompt: Vamos a comprar una casa. Who is 'we'?
hints: Vamos ends in -amos, the nosotros giveaway: we. The plan includes the speaker — that is the 'we'.
activities.feedback: vamos = we (nosotros) — the plan includes me. The ending -amos is the giveaway.

activities.prompt: Put the words in order: I am going to learn Italian.
hints: Conjugated ir first — Voy — then the bridge a, then the untouched infinitive aprender, then what: italiano. Voy a aprender italiano.
activities.feedback: Voy a aprender italiano — conjugated ir, then a, then the untouched infinitive. That order never changes.

activities.prompt: Translate into Spanish: We are going to travel in summer.
hints: We-plan = vamos + a + the infinitive: vamos a viajar. Then en verano pins the season. The bridge a never disappears.
activities.feedback: Vamos a viajar — we-plan in four syllables. En verano pins down when.

errors.explanation: Ir a needs its bridge a: Vamos a viajar en verano.
Only the first verb conjugates — after a comes the bare infinitive: vamos a viajar.
Voy is 'I'; the prompt says 'we' — Vamos a viajar en verano.

activities.prompt: ___ a venir a la fiesta? (tú, are you going to…)
hints: The invite checks the other person's plan: tú goes with vas. Vas a venir a la fiesta? — not voy.
activities.feedback: ¿Vas a venir? — the invitation check. Vas, not *voy: the plan is theirs, not yours.

errors.explanation: The plan is yours, not mine — tú takes vas: ¿Vas a venir a la fiesta?
Va is he/she; the question asks tú — vas.
Vamos is 'we'; the question asks you — vas.

activities.prompt: Read the life plan. Who is going to live with the narrator?
hints: The passage's third sentence: Mi hermana va a venir a vivir conmigo. The sister moves in — the new job and the Italian are separate plans.
activities.feedback: Mi hermana va a venir a vivir conmigo — va a, the third-person plan.

errors.explanation: The narrator is going to LOOK FOR a new job — the one moving in is the sister: mi hermana.
No mother appears here. The passage says mi hermana va a venir a vivir conmigo.
Summer is when they travel together; the person coming to live is her sister.

activities.prompt: ¿Podrías ayudarme? This is…
activities.feedback: a polite request — the conditional softens could you into asking, not telling. Commands bark; the conditional knocks.

activities.prompt: Predict: I would like → me ___.
activities.feedback: me gustaría — gustar's conditional. The politest I-want in the language, and worth owning cold.

activities.prompt: Which stem is irregular in the conditional?
activities.feedback: tendría — tener→tendr-, one of the same six rebels as the future. The rest keep the whole infinitive.

activities.prompt: Translate into Spanish: You should rest more. (tú)
activities.feedback: Deberías — advice wears the -ías ending for tú. Should, not must: gentle, not bossy.

activities.prompt: Read the dream trip. Where would the narrator go in spring?
activities.feedback: Iría a Japón en primavera — the conditional iría does the dreaming.

activities.body: Here is the pattern before the rule: when your wish lands on someone else, the second verb changes shape — Quiero que vengas, not *vienes. Build it from the yo present: drop the -o, add the opposite endings — hablo→hable→hables, como→coma→comas. Tattoo the triggers: quiero que, necesito que, es importante que.

activities.prompt: Quiero que vengas. Why vengas and not vienes?
hints: Quiero que puts the wish on someone else, and the second verb flips into the subjunctive: vengas. Keep the same subject and it stays an infinitive — Quiero venir.
activities.feedback: a wish on someone else — quiero que flips the second verb into the subjunctive. Same subject would stay infinitive: Quiero venir.

options.text: a wish on someone else triggers the subjunctive

activities.prompt: Predict the subjunctive: quiero que ___ (hablar, tú).
hints: The recipe from the intro: hablo → drop the -o → hable → add the tú -s → hables. The -es ending is the opposite-conjugation tell.
activities.feedback: hablo → hable → hables: drop the -o, add the opposite ending, then the tú -s. The recipe never changes.

errors.explanation: Hablas is the indicative; after a wish-trigger the verb flips to the subjunctive: hables.
Hable is the él/ella subjunctive; the tú form adds its -s: hables.
Hablo is the yo present; the wish lands on tú, who takes hables.

activities.prompt: Which trigger needs the subjunctive?
hints: Quiero que is a wish-trigger — it flips the next verb. Creo que, es verdad que and sé que keep the indicative: they state facts, not wishes.
activities.feedback: quiero que — wanting triggers it. creer, saber and es verdad keep the indicative: Creo que viene (fact, not wish).

activities.prompt: Put the words in order: I need you to help me.
hints: The trigger Necesito que leads, me rides before the subjunctive, then ayudes: Necesito que me ayudes.
activities.feedback: Necesito que me ayudes — the need, the que-bridge, then the subjunctive. Word order is mercifully simple.

activities.prompt: Translate into Spanish: It's important that you study. (tú)
hints: The impersonal trigger works exactly like quiero que: es importante que + the subjunctive. Estudiar → estudies for tú.
activities.feedback: Es importante que estudies — the impersonal trigger works exactly like quiero que.

errors.explanation: Estudias is the indicative — after the trigger the verb flips: estudies.
The trigger needs its que-bridge: Es importante que estudies.
Estudie is he/she; the tú form keeps its -s: estudies.

activities.prompt: Quiero que ___ a la fiesta. (venir, tú)
hints: The trigger is regular, the verb is not: venir's subjunctive stem is veng-. Tú takes the -as: vengas.
activities.feedback: Quiero que vengas — venir's subjunctive is irregular (veng-), but the trigger is perfectly regular.

errors.explanation: Vienes is the indicative — the intro's exact warning: Quiero que vengas, not vienes.
Vengo is the yo form; the wish lands on tú, who takes vengas.
Venga is he/she; the tú subjunctive of venir is vengas.

activities.prompt: Read the mother's rules. How many hours of sleep does she want?
hints: The mother's list ends with it: es importante que duermas ocho horas. The answer is the number of hours — ocho.
activities.feedback: es importante que duermas ocho horas — the subjunctive duermas carries the mother's wish.

errors.explanation: The passage says ocho horas, not four.
The mother wants eight hours of sleep — diez is not in her rules.
En paz is the narrator's own wish (que me deje en paz); the mother wants ocho horas.

activities.body: Stop writing two short sentences — glue them. El libro que leí. La ciudad donde vivo. La persona con quien hablé. Que does most of the work; quien steps in for people after prepositions; donde owns places; lo que wraps up whole ideas (Lo que dices es verdad).

activities.prompt: La persona con quien hablé. Why quien and not que?
activities.feedback: a person after a preposition — con + person demands quien. Without the preposition, que would do: la persona que vi.

activities.prompt: Predict: the city where I live → la ciudad ___ vivo.
activities.feedback: donde — places take donde. La ciudad donde vivo: the noun, the glue, the clause.

activities.prompt: Lo que dices es verdad. Lo que means…
activities.feedback: what — lo que wraps a whole idea: what you say. Who/when/where need their own words.

activities.prompt: Put the words in order: The book I read is great.
activities.feedback: El libro que leí es genial — noun, glue, clause, then the main verb. One sentence, two ideas.

activities.prompt: La persona con ___ hablé fue amable.
activities.feedback: con quien — person plus preposition. Que would work without con; with it, only quien.

activities.body: Comparison is one formula: más/menos + adjective + que; equality is tan + adjective + como. Four words refuse the formula and bring their own: mejor, peor, mayor, menor. And never stack them — *más mejor is the classic learner tattoo: mejor already means more good.

activities.prompt: Which sentence compares two things as equal?
hints: Equality wears tan…como: Es tan alto como su hermano. Más/menos…que compare unequally, and el más alto crowns — equality is the pair with tan.
activities.feedback: tan…como = as…as — equality. más/menos…que compare unequally; el más alto crowns him above all.

options.text: Es tan alto como su hermano.
Es más alto que su hermano.
Es menos alto que su hermano.

activities.prompt: Predict: better → ___.
hints: Bueno's rebel comparative is mejor — it replaces the formula, so más never stacks on it. Better = mejor, full stop.
activities.feedback: mejor — bueno's rebel form. Never *más bueno; the rebel replaces the formula.

errors.explanation: Bueno is the plain adjective 'good'; the comparative is the rebel mejor.
Never stack the formula on a rebel — mejor already means 'more good'. *Más bueno is the learner tattoo the intro warns about.
The blank wants the bare comparative mejor; la mejor turns it into 'the best (feminine)'.

activities.prompt: Más de tres personas. Why de and not que?
hints: Before a number, que switches to de: más de tres, menos de diez. It is not a typo — numbers get their own preposition.
activities.feedback: before a number, que becomes de: más de tres, menos de diez. Numbers get their own preposition.

options.text: before a number, que becomes de

activities.prompt: Put the words in order: Madrid is bigger than Seville.
hints: Subject, es, más, adjective, que, rival: Madrid es más grande que Sevilla. Que links the two sides of the comparison.
activities.feedback: Madrid es más grande que Sevilla — the formula in order: noun, es, más, adjective, que, rival.

activities.prompt: Translate into Spanish: My flat is less expensive than yours.
hints: Menos follows the same formula as más: menos caro que. 'Yours' stays a pronoun phrase — el tuyo — with no repeated noun.
activities.feedback: menos caro que — less follows the same formula as more. El tuyo = yours, no noun repeated.

answers: Mi piso es menos caro que el tuyo.

errors.answer: Mi piso es más caro que el tuyo.
errors.explanation: Más caro means more expensive — the prompt says less (menos): menos caro que.

errors.answer: Mi piso es menos caro que tuyo.
errors.explanation: Yours needs its el: que el tuyo.

errors.answer: Mi piso es menos caro que tú.
errors.explanation: Tú is the pronoun 'you'; 'yours' is the possessive el tuyo.

errors.answer: Mi piso es menos caro que tu.
errors.explanation: Tu without accent is 'your' + noun; the possessive 'yours' is el tuyo.

activities.prompt: Es ___ alto como su hermano. (as…)
hints: Equality opens with tan and closes with como — tan alto como. Más would demand que, and como alone cannot open the pair.
activities.feedback: tan…como — the equality pair. Tan opens it, como closes it.

errors.explanation: Tanto belongs before nouns (tanto dinero); before an adjective the form is tan: tan alto como.
Más pairs with que for inequality; the equality formula is tan…como.
Como closes the pair; tan opens it: tan alto como.

activities.prompt: Read the brothers. Who cooks better?
hints: The passage says it outright: yo cocino mejor que él — I cook better than him. The brother is taller and faster, but cooking belongs to the narrator.
activities.feedback: cocino mejor que él — I cook better than him. Mejor settles the kitchen debate.

errors.explanation: The brother is more athletic; the one who cooks better is the narrator.
The mother makes the comparison — she is not the cook. The narrator cooks mejor que él.
The father appears only in 'as stubborn as' — the better cook is the narrator.

activities.body: Fluent speakers don't repeat nouns — they swap in tiny pronouns that hug the verb: Lo veo, le di, me lo dio. Direct objects (what?) are lo/la/los/las; indirect objects (to whom?) are me/te/le/nos/os/les. When le meets lo they merge into se: se lo di. Short, fast, natural.

activities.prompt: Lo veo. What does lo replace?
activities.feedback: the direct object — lo stands in for what you see. The subject is the hidden yo; lo is never the doer.

activities.prompt: Predict: I gave it to him → se ___.
activities.feedback: se lo — the diplomat se plus lo. Never *le lo: Spanish melts that collision into se.

activities.prompt: Le di el libro a María. Le is…
activities.feedback: indirect — le = to her, the receiver. El libro is the direct object (what was given).

activities.prompt: Put the words in order: He gave it to me yesterday.
activities.feedback: Me lo dio ayer — indirect, direct, verb, when. Both pronouns hug the verb, in that order.

activities.prompt: ___ di el libro. (to him: I gave…)
activities.feedback: Le di — to him. Even with a María named later, le marks the receiver up front.

activities.body: Por looks backward — the cause, the exchange, the way through: por eso, gracias por, por Madrid. Para looks forward — the purpose, the destination, the deadline: para aprender, para ti, para mañana. One question splits them: am I explaining why, or intending what?

activities.prompt: Estudio para aprender. Para here marks…
hints: Para aprender = in order to learn — the goal ahead: purpose. Causes, exchanges and movement through belong to por.
activities.feedback: purpose — para aprender = in order to learn, the goal ahead. Causes and movement belong to por.

activities.prompt: Predict: Thanks for your help → gracias ___ tu ayuda.
hints: Gratitude looks backward — gracias por tu ayuda. The help already happened, so por, never para.
activities.feedback: gracias por — por looks back at what you're thankful for. The help already happened.

errors.explanation: Para looks forward; gratitude looks back at the help that already happened — gracias por.
De does not carry gratitude; the thanks-for pair is gracias por.
Porque starts a clause ('because'); the blank wants the preposition por: gracias por tu ayuda.

activities.prompt: Lo hice por ti. Por here means…
hints: Por ti names the cause behind the action: because of you. The destination reading would be para ti — but this sentence has no destination.
activities.feedback: because of you — por ti names the cause behind the action. The recipient reading (*for you as destination) would be para ti.

activities.prompt: Put the words in order: It's for you.
hints: The recipient gets para: Es para ti. Three words — subject, verb, para + pronoun.
activities.feedback: Es para ti — the recipient gets para. Three words, one direction: forward.

activities.prompt: Translate into Spanish: I need it for tomorrow.
hints: A deadline looks forward: para mañana. Lo carries the 'it' and rides before the verb: Lo necesito para mañana.
activities.feedback: para mañana — the deadline reading of para. By tomorrow, not because of tomorrow.

errors.explanation: A deadline looks forward — por mañana would mean 'because of tomorrow' or 'by tomorrow' in the wrong sense: para mañana.
The 'it' needs its pronoun lo before the verb: Lo necesito para mañana.
The neutral 'it' here is lo, not la: Lo necesito para mañana.

activities.prompt: Paso ___ Madrid para ver a mi hermana. (through…)
hints: Passing through a place is movement through space: por Madrid. The para later in the sentence marks the purpose of the stop.
activities.feedback: por Madrid = through Madrid — movement through space. Then para ver: the purpose of the stop.

segments.text: Madrid para ver a mi hermana.

errors.explanation: Para marks the purpose — para ver a mi hermana. Movement through a city is por: por Madrid.
De is 'of/from'; passing through a city wears por: Paso por Madrid.
En is 'in/at'; the journey through Madrid is por: Paso por Madrid.

activities.prompt: Read the trip. When does the narrator return?
hints: The last line answers it: Vuelvo el lunes por la noche. Monday is the return day, and por la noche tells you when on Monday.
activities.feedback: Vuelvo el lunes por la noche — por la noche is por's time-of-day reading: in/during the night.

errors.explanation: Mañana is when the trip STARTS (salgo de viaje); the return is el lunes por la noche.
The trip-home happens por la noche, not por la mañana — the last line says so.
Por la noche alone names the time of day; the return DAY is lunes — el lunes por la noche.

activities.body: To crown the best, put el/la/los/las in front of más: el más alto, la más rápida, los más amables. For the extreme, weld -ísimo onto the adjective: buenísimo, grandísima, altísimo. And the words of work — la entrevista, el jefe, el sueldo, el horario — because superlatives shine brightest in interviews.

activities.prompt: Which sentence is a superlative?
hints: A superlative crowns with el más…de: Es el más alto de la clase. Más…que only compares two, and tan…como declares equality.
activities.feedback: Es el más alto de la clase — el más…de crowns him above all. más…que only compares two; tan…como declares equality.

options.text: Es el más alto de la clase.

activities.prompt: Predict the -ísimo form of bueno.
hints: Bueno drops its -o and welds on -ísimo: buenísimo. Extreme good in a single word.
activities.feedback: bueno → buenísimo: drop the -o, weld on -ísimo. Extreme good, one word.

errors.explanation: Bueno is the plain adjective; the -ísimo extreme of it is buenísimo.
Muy bueno means 'very good'; the -ísimo form is the extreme in one word: buenísimo.
The -ísimo ending carries its accent: buenísimo.

activities.prompt: La oficina es grandísima. Grandísima means…
hints: -ísima cranks grande to the extreme — huge. It is a megaphone, not a shrinker: 'big-ish', 'small' and 'new' are all wrong.
activities.feedback: huge — -ísima cranks grande to the extreme. It's not a diminutive; it's a megaphone.

activities.prompt: Put the words in order: I have an interview tomorrow.
hints: Have, what, when: Tengo una entrevista mañana. The verb leads and the when trails.
activities.feedback: Tengo una entrevista mañana — have, what, when. The job hunt in four words.

activities.prompt: Translate into Spanish: My schedule is flexible.
hints: El horario is masculine and states of things ride ser: Mi horario es flexible. Hora would be the wrong noun — that is the hour, not the schedule.
activities.feedback: Mi horario es flexible — el horario, masculine. States of things wear ser.

errors.explanation: Being flexible is what the schedule is, not a temporary state — ser: es flexible.
Horario is singular, so the adjective is singular too: flexible.
Hora is the hour or time; the schedule is el horario.

activities.prompt: Mis compañeros son ___ más amables del mundo.
hints: The article must match compañeros — masculine plural: los más amables. El, la or las would break the agreement.
activities.feedback: los — the article must match compañeros (masculine plural). El más…de needs its article to agree.

errors.explanation: Compañeros is plural, so the article is los: los más amables.
Compañeros is masculine — the article is los, not las.
La is feminine singular; compañeros needs the masculine plural los.

activities.prompt: Read the new job. How many days a week does the narrator work?
hints: The passage ends with the schedule: trabajo cuatro días por semana. The answer is the number — cuatro.
activities.feedback: trabajo cuatro días por semana — and calls the schedule buenísimo. The superlative earns its keep.

errors.explanation: A five-day week is the usual guess, but the passage says cuatro días por semana.
The office is downtown — the question asks how many days he works: cuatro.
Buenísimo describes the schedule; the question asks how many days — cuatro.

activities.body:
Tonight you check into a hotel in Madrid. Your mission:
— Greet reception: Hola, buenas tardes.
— Confirm your booking: Tengo una reserva a nombre de García.
— Ask about breakfast: ¿A qué hora es el desayuno?
— Report a problem: No hay agua caliente.
— Ask for another key: ¿Me puede dar otra llave, por favor?

activities.prompt: You walk up to the reception desk. What do you say first?
hints: Check-in opens with a greeting: Hola plus the evening greeting buenas tardes. Adiós and me voy belong to the end of the stay.
activities.feedback: Hola, buenas tardes opens every interaction. Adiós closes it, gracias thanks for something, and me voy leaves — greet first.

activities.prompt: The receptionist asks for your name. Say: I have a reservation under García.
hints: Say what you have, then the fixed booking phrase: Tengo + una reserva + a nombre de + your surname — a nombre de never changes.
activities.feedback: Tengo una reserva a nombre de… — have + reservation + under + name. A nombre de is the fixed phrase; don't improvise it.

answers: Tengo una reserva a nombre de García.

errors.answer: Tengo una reserva con nombre de García.
errors.explanation: The fixed phrase is a nombre de ('under the name of'), not con: Tengo una reserva a nombre de García.

errors.answer: Tengo una reserva nombre de García.
errors.explanation: The a in a nombre de is part of the fixed phrase: a nombre de García.

errors.answer: Tengo reserva a nombre de García.
errors.explanation: Una belongs with reserva: Tengo una reserva.

activities.prompt: Build the question: What time is breakfast?
hints: The time question leads with ¿A qué hora, then the verb es, then el desayuno — one line.
activities.feedback: ¿A qué hora es el desayuno? — the a belongs to the question word; el desayuno is what you're asking about.

activities.prompt: The shower runs cold. Which complaint fits?
hints: Your complaint must name what is missing: hot water is agua caliente. Only one line does that — no hay agua caliente.
activities.feedback: No hay agua caliente names the missing thing. The others complain about breakfast, the key, the desk — not your shower.

activities.prompt: Complete the complaint about the room.
hints: 'The room has no ___ caliente' — the missing noun is the water itself: agua caliente.
activities.feedback: No hay agua caliente / no tiene agua caliente — name what's missing and the desk fixes it. Report, don't apologize.

errors.explanation: Caliente ('hot') is already at the end of the sentence — the missing word is the water itself: agua.
Caliente comes after the blank; write only the noun agua: no tiene agua caliente.

activities.prompt: Build: Can you give me another key, please?
hints: The polite ask opens ¿Me puede dar, then the object otra llave, then por favor.
activities.feedback: ¿Me puede dar otra llave, por favor? — can-you-give-me, then what, then por favor softens the landing.

activities.prompt: Checkout is easy: tell them the room is very good.
hints: How the room is right now takes estar: La habitación + está muy bien.
activities.feedback: Está, not es — how the room is right now wears estar. Muy bien does the praising.

errors.explanation: How the room is right now takes estar, not ser: La habitación está muy bien.
Bien is the adverb that goes with está ('is well'); bueno is an adjective that describes a noun: está muy bien.
The article la opens the sentence: La habitación está muy bien.

activities.prompt: Morning, and you're hungry. From memory now: ask about breakfast.
hints: The breakfast question you built in step 4 — now from memory: ¿A qué hora es el desayuno?
activities.feedback: ¿A qué hora es el desayuno? — you built it in step 4; now it comes from memory. That is the mission working.

errors.explanation: Event times use es, not está: ¿A qué hora es el desayuno?
The a is part of the question-word group: ¿A qué hora…?
The article el sits before desayuno: el desayuno.

activities.body: Tech Spanish is refreshingly regular: enviar → envío, descargar → descarga. The nouns are the real lesson — el móvil, la contraseña, la pantalla, el wifi — and one golden contraction: de + el always melts into del. La contraseña del wifi, never *de el wifi.

activities.prompt: Which sentence asks for the wifi password?
hints: Cuál asks which one — the password itself: ¿Cuál es la contraseña del wifi? Dónde looks for a place, qué for a definition, cuánto for a price.
activities.feedback: ¿Cuál es…? asks which one it is — the password itself. Dónde asks where, qué asks what it is, cuánto asks the price.

activities.prompt: Predict the yo present of enviar: te ___ un mensaje.
hints: Enviar is regular: yo → envío, with the accent on the í. Tech verbs rarely surprise you — learn the noun and the verb behaves.
activities.feedback: enviar is regular: envío. Tech verbs rarely surprise you — learn the noun, the verb behaves.

errors.explanation: The yo present carries its accent: envío.
Envió is the past; the present yo form is envío.
Envía is he/she; the 'te ___ un mensaje' from me is envío.

activities.prompt: La contraseña del wifi. Del = …
hints: De + el always melts into del — the intro's golden contraction. De el wifi is wrong in every register.
activities.feedback: de + el — the mandatory contraction. *De el wifi is always wrong, in every register.

activities.prompt: Put the words in order: Download the app.
hints: Commands lead with the verb: Descarga, then the article + noun la aplicación. Descarga la aplicación.
activities.feedback: Descarga la aplicación — command, then what. Imperatives lead with the verb.

activities.prompt: Translate into Spanish: The screen is broken.
hints: Broken is a state, so estar: está. Pantalla is feminine, so the adjective agrees: rota, not roto.
activities.feedback: La pantalla está rota — broken states wear estar, not ser. La pantalla is feminine: rota, not roto.

errors.explanation: Being broken is a state, so estar, not ser: está rota.
Pantalla is feminine, so the adjective is rota: está rota.
Pantalla is feminine, so the article is la: La pantalla está rota.

activities.prompt: Te ___ el documento. (enviar, yo)
hints: Te rides before the verb, and enviar's yo present needs its accent: envío. Te envío el documento.
activities.feedback: Te envío — the indirect pronoun te rides before the verb: I send it to you.

errors.explanation: The yo present of enviar carries its accent: envío.
Envió is the past 'he sent'; the present yo form is envío.
Envía is he/she sends; the prompt says yo — envío.

activities.prompt: Read the phone saga. What did the technician say was fine?
hints: The technician's verdict is the battery: la batería está bien. The screen broke and the system needed the update — the battery was the part that was fine.
activities.feedback: la batería está bien — está, because it's a state. The fix was the update, not the battery.

errors.explanation: The screen is what BROKE — the technician said la batería está bien.
The system is what needed the update — the part that was fine is the battery.
The update was downloaded afterwards; what the technician declared fine was la batería.

activities.body: You are lost two streets from the Museo del Prado, and your phone just died. Your mission: stop a passerby, ask where the museum is, follow the directions — straight ahead, then left — and close with a polite Perdone. Tools: ¿Dónde está…?, todo recto, a la izquierda, luego.

activities.prompt: You stop a passerby. Which question asks where the museum is?
hints: A where-question leads with the asking word ¿Dónde, then the verb está, then the place — the museum line does all three: ¿Dónde está el museo?
activities.feedback: ¿Dónde está el museo? — the asking word first, then está, then the place. The accent on dónde is there because the word is asking.

activities.prompt: The passerby answers: «Todo recto, luego a la izquierda.» What do you do?
hints: Luego means 'then' — the direction you hear first is the one you do first: straight ahead, and only afterwards the left turn.
activities.feedback: Todo recto first, then — luego — a la izquierda. Follow the order the words give you.

activities.body: Saturday market, and your shopping list has three lines: un kilo de manzanas, una botella de agua, medio kilo de queso. Your mission: ask for each by quantity — every quantity brings its de — point with este or esta, and be home by noon.

activities.prompt: You point at the apples and want a kilo. Which line is right?
hints: Apples are feminine and plural, so the pointer is Estas — and the quantity keeps its de: un kilo de manzanas.
activities.feedback: Manzanas is feminine and plural, so the pointer is estas. The quantity keeps its de: un kilo de manzanas.

options.text: Estas manzanas: un kilo, por favor.
Estos manzanas: un kilo, por favor.
Esta manzanas: un kilo, por favor.
Este manzanas: un kilo, por favor.

activities.body: Your head is pounding and the hotel has nothing. Your mission: walk into the pharmacy, ask ¿Tiene algo para…?, state what you need with Necesito…, and check Es sin receta — no prescription needed. Remember: para is the purpose word, never por.

activities.prompt: The pharmacist asks «¿Necesita algo más?» You need nothing else. Which reply fits?
hints: You have what you need, so refuse politely — No, gracias. Sí would invite more.
activities.feedback: No, gracias — the clean no. Sí would ask for more; por favor belongs on a request, not a refusal.

activities.body: Saturday night at the café. You meet Pablo and want him at your dinner. He will answer warmly — ¡Claro que sí! — or decline gently: Lo siento, no puedo. Your lines: ¿Quieres venir?, Te invito a cenar.

activities.prompt: Pablo: «¿Qué haces el sábado?» Choose your reply.
activities.feedback: Te invito a cenar el sábado — warm, direct, and the a is doing its job.

options.text: Te invito a cenar el sábado.
options.feedback: The invitation lands: te invito a — the a bridges invito to the event.
That un-invites him. Warm and direct is the Spanish way — save the no for later.
Dónde asks where a place is; Saturday is a when, not a where.
Too blunt — and it invites nothing. Te invito a… opens the door.

activities.prompt: Pablo: «¡Claro que sí! ¿A qué hora?» Choose your reply.
activities.feedback: A las ocho. ¿Vienes? — you set the time and keep him in the conversation.

options.feedback: Time plus the gentle check — the conversation flows.
He just accepted; walking away now would be very strange.
A no without a reason kills the invitation you just made.
You asked the time — but he asked you. Answer first.

activities.body: A Seville market stall. You love the olives; the price surprises you. Your lines: ¿Cuánto cuesta?, Es caro, La cuenta, por favor — and cuesta agrees with one thing, cuestan with several.

activities.prompt: Seller: «¿Cuánto quiere?» (how much do you want) Choose your reply.
activities.feedback: Un kilo, por favor — quantity first, courtesy always.

options.feedback: A quantity with por favor — the perfect market answer.
Mucho of what? The seller needs a quantity, not an appetite.
That is the seller’s line, not yours.
You just walked up to the stall — at least name a quantity first.

activities.prompt: The seller says «Son dos euros.» You want to haggle politely. Which line works?
activities.feedback: ¿Me lo deja en uno cincuenta? — will you leave it for me at 1.50. Polite haggling, not a complaint.

activities.prompt: Seller: «¿Algo más?» Choose your reply.
activities.feedback: No, gracias. La cuenta, por favor — done shopping, settling up.

options.text: No, gracias. La cuenta, por favor.
options.feedback: The clean finish: decline, then ask for the bill.
Sí and no in one breath — the seller will stare.
Asking for it to be more expensive is… a bold strategy.
Adiós is for leaving, and it never takes cuenta with it.

activities.body: A busy café, a rushed waiter. Politeness is your superpower: poder and querer take the infinitive — Puedo ir, Quiero comer — and the conditional softens everything: Querría un café, por favor.

activities.prompt: Waiter: «¿Qué van a tomar?» Choose your reply.
activities.feedback: Querría un café, por favor — the softened verb does the heavy lifting.

options.feedback: The conditional in its best clothes — courteous to the last syllable.
An order barked, not asked. The waiter will remember you — badly.
Quiero is blunt; ahora makes it a demand.
Word order scrambled — and still blunt.

activities.prompt: Waiter: «¿Necesitan algo más?» Choose your reply.
activities.feedback: ¿Puedes traerme la cuenta, por favor? — can, not command.

options.feedback: Poder plus infinitive plus por favor — textbook polite.
The imperative with a rushed waiter is a risk.
Blunt and backwards. Ya never hurries a waiter helpfully.
Adiós ends the conversation, not the bill.

activities.body: You are the new kid in class and want friends fast. Your tool: questions — qué, quién, dónde, cuándo, cómo — every one wearing its accent, question word first, then the verb.

activities.prompt: Lucía: «Soy de Valencia.» Choose your follow-up.
activities.feedback: ¿Dónde vives ahora? — dónde for where, accent on, question word first.

options.feedback: Dónde asks where — the natural follow-up to where someone is from.
Qué asks what; you cannot what-live somewhere.
Cuándo asks when — she just told you where, not when.
The question word must lead: ¿Dónde vives ahora?

activities.prompt: Lucía: «¿Y tú?» Choose your reply.
activities.feedback: Me llamo Sam. ¿Cómo te llamas? — answer, then ask back.

options.feedback: Name first, then the question back — the accent on cómo asks how.
Qué asks what; names are asked with cómo.
Llamarse is reflexive — me llamo, not llamo.
Word salad. Me llamo Sam keeps the order: verb, then name.

activities.body: Ana invites you home, and her family is curious. Your lines: Me llamo…, Tengo un hermano, Esta es mi familia. Remember: el hermano, la hermana — the article shows the gender — and mi becomes mis when you count more than one.

activities.prompt: Ana’s mother: «¿Cómo te llamas?» Choose your reply.
activities.feedback: Me llamo Alex. ¿Y usted? — introduce, then return the courtesy.

options.feedback: Me llamo plus the polite return — usted for the mother you just met.
Es wandered in from another sentence. Me llamo Alex needs no es.
The reflexive pronoun leads: me llamo, never llamo me.
Qué cannot ask a name; cómo with its accent does.

activities.prompt: Ana: «¿Tienes hermanos?» Choose your reply.
activities.feedback: Sí, tengo un hermano — tengo, then the brother with his article.

options.feedback: Tener is irregular — tengo, never tene — and un hermano keeps its masculine article.
Uno shortens to un before a masculine noun: un hermano.
El points at a specific brother; un introduces yours.
Verb before object: tengo hermanos, not the reverse.

activities.body: Your friend is stressed about exams. Advise softly, wish boldly: the conditional is the future with a softer ending — hablaría, comería, tendría, podría. It dreams (viajaría), it advises (deberías), and it softens every request (¿Podrías ayudarme?).

activities.prompt: Friend: «Estoy agotado.» (I’m exhausted.) Choose your reply.
activities.feedback: Deberías descansar más — the conditional advises without ordering.

options.feedback: Advice wears the -ías ending — should, not must: gentle, not bossy.
The imperative barks; an exhausted friend needs the conditional’s softness.
Debes is must — stronger than asked for, and ya hurries nobody.
Never rest is the opposite of advice.

activities.prompt: Friend: «¿Me ayudas con el examen?» Choose your reply.
activities.feedback: Claro. ¿Podrías venir mañana? — yes, wrapped in courtesy.

options.feedback: Claro agrees; podrías softens the ask into a question, not a demand.
An order in return for a request — the friendship will notice.
Nunca slams the door; a softer no exists.
Imperative plus ya — a command, not a conversation.

activities.prompt: Build the sentence: my books are on the table.
activities.feedback: Mis libros están en la mesa — plural noun, so mi becomes mis; the rest is furniture.

activities.prompt: Build the sentence: the tables are big.
activities.feedback: Las mesas son grandes — vowel ending takes -s, and the article turns feminine plural: las.

activities.prompt: Build the sentence: she never eats meat.
activities.feedback: Ella nunca come carne — nunca can open or follow; the no stays glued before the verb it denies.

activities.prompt: Build the sentence: the house where I was born is old.
activities.feedback: La casa donde nací es vieja — donde glues the place to its clause; one sentence, two ideas.

activities.prompt: Build the sentence: she gave it to me this morning.
activities.feedback: Me lo dio esta mañana — indirect, direct, verb, when. Both pronouns hug the verb, in that order.

activities.body: 6:45 am. Leo’s alarm rings in Madrid, and his whole day runs on a small machine: remove -ar, add -o for I, -a for he or she — trabajo, trabaja, estudio, estudia. The clock is always por: por la mañana, por la tarde, por la noche. Follow his day.
Por la tarde everything shifts: Leo studies Spanish and his sister works. Por la noche the city slows, the lights come on — and Leo finally asks what his day was made of.

activities.prompt: Leo writes his diary. Complete his day in Spanish: I work in the morning and study at night.
hints: Chain both halves with y — trabajo and estudio each keep their -o ending, and each half keeps its por la phrase: por la mañana … por la noche.
activities.feedback: Trabajo por la mañana y estudio por la noche — the -o ending is yours, and por carries the time.

answers: Trabajo por la mañana y estudio por la noche.

errors.answer: Trabaja por la mañana y estudio por la noche.
errors.explanation: The diary is yours — 'I work' takes the -o form: Trabajo por la mañana.

errors.answer: Trabajo por la mañana y estudia por la noche.
errors.explanation: 'I study' keeps your -o ending: … y estudio por la noche.

errors.answer: Trabajo por mañana y estudio por noche.
errors.explanation: Both time phrases keep their article: por la mañana, por la noche.

activities.body: Moving day. Ana’s family carries boxes into the new flat: la cocina, el dormitorio, el salón, el baño. In Spanish no noun travels alone — it carries its article, and the article tells the gender: el, la, los, las. Watch a and de fuse with el: al, del.
By evening the boxes are gone. Ana walks from room to room — Vengo del salón, voy a la cocina — and the flat finally feels like home.

activities.prompt: Ana texts her friend about the flat. Write in Spanish: the kitchen is big and the bedrooms are small.
hints: Two clauses joined by y: the kitchen is feminine singular (la cocina es grande) and the bedrooms are masculine plural (los dormitorios son pequeños) — match each verb to its noun.
activities.feedback: La cocina es grande y los dormitorios son pequeños — feminine singular la, masculine plural los, adjective matching both.

answers: La cocina es grande y los dormitorios son pequeños.

errors.answer: La cocina es grande y las dormitorios son pequeños.
errors.explanation: Dormitorios is masculine, so its plural article is los: los dormitorios son pequeños.

errors.answer: La cocina es grande y los dormitorios es pequeños.
errors.explanation: A plural noun needs the plural verb son: los dormitorios son pequeños.

errors.answer: El cocina es grande y los dormitorios son pequeños.
errors.explanation: Cocina is feminine — la cocina, just as in the moving-day tour.

activities.body: Sunday, 2 pm. The García family sits down together: la comida, el pan, el agua, la fruta, el queso. They eat (comer), they drink (beber), and everything they love gets the backwards verb: me gusta.
Dessert arrives — la fruta and el queso. Everyone has a favourite, me gusta is doing overtime, and nobody is leaving the table yet.

activities.prompt: You join the table. Write in Spanish: I like the bread and I drink water.
hints: Two halves joined by y: the backwards liking keeps its article (Me gusta el pan) and the drinking stays straight with your -o (bebo agua).
activities.feedback: Me gusta el pan y bebo agua — liking is backwards (the bread pleases me), drinking is straightforward.

answers: Me gusta el pan y bebo agua.

errors.answer: Me gusta pan y bebo agua.
errors.explanation: The liked thing keeps its article: Me gusta el pan.

errors.answer: Me gusto el pan y bebo agua.
errors.explanation: Me gusto would be 'I please myself' — the bread pleases me, so gusta: Me gusta el pan.

errors.answer: Me gusta el pan y bebe agua.
errors.explanation: You drink, so keep your -o ending: … y bebo agua.

activities.body: 8 am. Marta must cross Madrid: first el metro, then el autobús, and the last stretch a pie. Her verb is ir — voy, vas, va — and her question all morning is ¿cómo voy?
The metro is packed. Marta switches plans: en coche with her brother through the traffic, then a pie through the old town, where the streets are too narrow for cars anyway.

activities.prompt: Marta arrives at last. Write in Spanish: I go by subway and then on foot.
hints: Keep your I form (voy), ride the metro with en, and switch to the fixed a pie after luego: Voy en metro y luego a pie.
activities.feedback: Voy en metro y luego a pie — ir for the going, en for the vehicle, a pie for your own two feet.

answers: Voy en metro y luego a pie.

errors.answer: Voy en metro y luego en pie.
errors.explanation: On foot is the fixed a pie: … y luego a pie.

errors.answer: Va en metro y luego a pie.
errors.explanation: You travel, so your -o form comes first: Voy en metro….

errors.answer: Voy a metro y luego a pie.
errors.explanation: The metro is a vehicle and rides on en: Voy en metro….

activities.body: The plan was the beach; the sky has other ideas. Hace sol in Madrid, está nublado in Valencia, hace frío in the mountains. Spanish weather is made, not been: hace plus a noun, está plus an adjective.
By afternoon the rain reaches Madrid too. The friends check the calendar — primavera, verano, otoño, invierno — and replan the whole trip around the forecast.

activities.prompt: You message a friend about the trip. Write in Spanish: it is sunny here and cold in the mountains.
hints: Both halves are made with hace: hace sol and hace frío. Here is aquí, and the mountains keep their article — en las montañas.
activities.feedback: Hace sol aquí y hace frío en las montañas — weather is made with hace, and aquí anchors it here.

answers: Hace sol aquí y hace frío en las montañas.

errors.answer: Hace sol aquí y hace frío en montañas.
errors.explanation: The mountains keep their article: en las montañas.

errors.answer: Es sol aquí y hace frío en las montañas.
errors.explanation: Sunny weather is made with hace: Hace sol aquí.

errors.answer: Hace sol aquí y está frío en las montañas.
errors.explanation: The cold here is made with hace too: … y hace frío.

activities.body: Monday morning. Pablo wakes up wrong: Me duele la cabeza. Spanish pain is backwards, just like Spanish liking — the head hurts to me. One aching part takes duele, several take duelen, and body parts wear the article, never a possessive: la cabeza, las manos.
By noon his hands hurt too, and his mother stops guessing: Voy al médico. At the clinic the nurse asks where it hurts, and Pablo finally has the words.

activities.prompt: At the clinic Pablo explains himself. Write in Spanish: my head hurts and I have a fever.
hints: Two complaints joined by y: the single aching head takes me duele la cabeza, and the fever is what you carry — tengo fiebre.
activities.feedback: Me duele la cabeza y tengo fiebre — duele for the single aching head, tengo for the fever you carry.

answers: Me duele la cabeza y tengo fiebre.

errors.answer: Me duele la cabeza y estoy fiebre.
errors.explanation: The fever is carried with tener: … y tengo fiebre.

errors.answer: Me duele la cabeza y tengo la fiebre.
errors.explanation: Fiebre takes no article here: … y tengo fiebre.

errors.answer: Me duele mi cabeza y tengo fiebre.
errors.explanation: Body parts take the article, not a possessive: Me duele la cabeza.

activities.body: At the feria, a fortune teller reads your palm. She promises — Te llamaré esta noche. She predicts — Mañana lloverá. She wonders about right now — ¿Dónde estará? The future does all three jobs.
Her last prediction is personal, and the forecast words gather round: creo que, probablemente, seguro, quizá — they turn plain statements into prophecies.

activities.prompt: You tell a friend your fortune. Write in Spanish: she will probably come tomorrow.
hints: Lead with the forecast word probablemente, then venir's future form vendrá (accented), then mañana — the predicting job in action: Probablemente vendrá mañana.
activities.feedback: Probablemente vendrá mañana — the forecast word first, then the future doing its predicting job.

errors.explanation: Viene is the present; a forecast about tomorrow takes the future vendrá.
The infinitive venir needs its future form: vendrá.
The future form carries its accent: vendrá.

activities.body: The narrator opens a photo album: De niño jugaba al fútbol. The imperfecto is the movie camera — era, iba, jugaba paint the scene while the action happens. The pretérito just snaps it: habló, jugué.
One photo freezes the square: Había mucha gente en la plaza. Every day he walked to school — iba a la escuela a pie — and the summers went on forever.

activities.prompt: Close the album. Write in Spanish: when I was a kid I used to play football every day.
hints: Keep the camera running: de niño (or cuando era niño) sets the scene, the daily habit takes jugaba, and football keeps its little al — De niño jugaba al fútbol todos los días.
activities.feedback: De niño jugaba al fútbol todos los días — jugaba keeps the habit running; the pretérito would have ended it.

answers: De niño jugaba al fútbol todos los días.
Cuando era niño jugaba al fútbol todos los días.

errors.answer: De niño jugué al fútbol todos los días.
errors.explanation: 'Every day' is a habit — the imperfecto jugaba, not the finished jugué.

errors.answer: Cuando era niño juego al fútbol todos los días.
errors.explanation: Juego is the present; the childhood habit takes jugaba.

errors.answer: De niño jugaba fútbol todos los días.
errors.explanation: Football keeps its little al: jugaba al fútbol.
