lessons.title: Misión: un café en Madrid
lessons.objective: Walk into a Madrid café and order a coffee — your first real conversation in Spanish.

lessons.title: Introducing yourself
lessons.objective: Introduce yourself with the reflexive verb llamarse and ask a name with the pronoun that travels with it.

legacyExercises.prompt: Me llamo Ana and Soy Ana both give a name. Which one uses the verb that literally means 'I call myself'?
legacyExercises.explanation: Me llamo Ana is the reflexive form — 'I call myself Ana'. Soy Ana uses ser ('to be'), and ¿Cómo te llamas? is the question.

legacyExercises.prompt: Ask a classmate their name with the question whose pronoun changes to te.
legacyExercises.explanation: The verb is the same one as in Me llamo, but the pronoun turns into te when it points at the person you are speaking to.

legacyExercises.prompt: Read the exchange. Which short word tells you the first speaker is talking about herself?
legacyExercises.explanation: Me is the reflexive pronoun: it turns the verb llamarse back on the person speaking. The other introduction uses soy instead.
legacyExercises.passage:
— ¡Hola! Me llamo Ana.
— Mucho gusto, Ana. Soy Leo.
— Encantada, Leo.
legacyExercises.translation:
— Hello! My name is Ana.
— Nice to meet you, Ana. I am Leo.
— Nice to meet you, Leo.

legacyExercises.prompt: A neighbour introduces herself to you. Give the two-word Spanish reply that closes an introduction.
legacyExercises.explanation: Mucho gusto closes an introduction, and the sentence needs no pronoun.

legacyExercises.prompt: The words are jumbled. Build the reflexive sentence that gives Ana's name.
legacyExercises.explanation: Me llamo Ana puts the reflexive pronoun first, then the verb, then the name.

legacyExercises.prompt: A classmate has introduced herself. Introduce yourself the same way, as Ana, using the verb that needs a pronoun.
legacyExercises.explanation: Say the whole reflexive phrase; leaving out me would leave the verb belonging to nobody.

lessons.culturalNote: The name question uses informal te for a peer. In a more formal situation, Spanish also has an usted form; this lesson stays with the informal question.

lessons.title: At the café
lessons.objective: Ask for a drink with the softened verb quisiera, and keep the accents on café and té.

legacyExercises.prompt: Quiero and quisiera are the same verb. Which request is the softened, polite one?
legacyExercises.explanation: Quisiera gives the verb a conditional ending, and that is what makes the request courteous. Quiero is the blunt form.

legacyExercises.prompt: Ask for tea politely, using the softened verb rather than quiero.
legacyExercises.explanation: Same polite frame, tea instead of coffee: Quisiera un té, por favor, with the accent on té.

legacyExercises.prompt: Read the café exchange. How many drinks does the customer order?
legacyExercises.explanation: The customer asks for a té and then adds un café, so two drinks in all.
legacyExercises.passage:
— ¡Buenas! Quisiera un té, por favor.
— ¿Un té?
— Sí, y un café también. Gracias.
legacyExercises.translation:
— Hello! I would like a tea, please.
— A tea?
— Yes, and a coffee too. Thank you.

answers: I would like a coffee, please.
legacyExercises.prompt: What does this café line mean in English: Quisiera un café, por favor.
legacyExercises.explanation: Quisiera is 'I would like', and por favor supplies the 'please'.

legacyExercises.prompt: Put the words in order to build the polite request for one coffee.
legacyExercises.explanation: Quisiera opens it, the drink follows with un, and por favor finishes the request.

legacyExercises.prompt: You reach the counter and want a coffee. Make the short polite request, without the verb.
legacyExercises.explanation: Un café, por favor — the short request drops quisiera but keeps por favor.

lessons.culturalNote: A greeting before a request and thanks afterward make this small exchange courteous.

lessons.title: Numbers and quantities
lessons.objective: Count one to ten, then see how Spanish welds a whole number such as veintiuno into a single written word.

legacyExercises.prompt: Three is hiding inside veintitrés, glued to veinte. Which Spanish word is it?
legacyExercises.explanation: Tres is three. The twenties simply glue a number onto veinte, so veintitrés is twenty-three.

legacyExercises.prompt: Read the price board. How much is the tea?
legacyExercises.explanation: The board prices tea at tres euros. Dos and tres behave here exactly as they did when you counted.
legacyExercises.passage:
Café: dos euros.
Té: tres euros.
legacyExercises.translation:
Coffee: two euros.
Tea: three euros.

legacyExercises.prompt: Put the Spanish words in order to ask the price of one coffee.
legacyExercises.explanation: ¿Cuánto cuesta? is the price question as a unit, and the upside-down question mark opens the sentence. Un café follows it.

legacyExercises.prompt: Say in Spanish: Two apples, please.
legacyExercises.explanation: Manzanas is feminine plural, so 'one' would be una, but two is dos either way, only the word for one changes with the noun.

legacyExercises.prompt: Think: a fruit seller has one apple but no sign. Ask the price in Spanish, then write the question.
legacyExercises.explanation: One apple is una manzana, with the feminine una. The price question itself never changes.

lessons.culturalNote: Prices may be said quickly. First listen for the number, then the item and the total.

lessons.title: Asking the way
lessons.objective: Learn the accent that turns donde into a question, then trace a set of directions step by step.
lessons.culturalNote: In Spain you open a request to a stranger with Perdone, and you thank them even for one sentence of directions.

lessons.title: Prices and paying
lessons.objective: Ask a price inside Spanish's two question marks, and make costar agree with one thing or with several.
lessons.culturalNote: In many Spanish bars the bill comes when you ask for it, so la cuenta, por favor is the normal way to end a meal.

lessons.title: Days and times
lessons.objective: Five Spanish weekdays are the old planets and gods; learn which two days break that pattern.

legacyExercises.prompt: Your Madrid phone writes a label above the date. Tap the label for today.
legacyExercises.explanation: That is hoy. The decoys mean tomorrow, Monday and the week.

legacyExercises.prompt: Build the Spanish sentence for on Monday I work; the article carries the on.
legacyExercises.explanation: El sits in front of the day and means on: el lunes, on Monday.

legacyExercises.prompt: Complete the Spanish for on Mondays, meaning every Monday: ___ lunes trabajo.
legacyExercises.explanation: Spanish uses the plural article for a repeated day: los lunes, on Mondays.

legacyExercises.prompt: Predict the sentence before you write it: today is Friday.
legacyExercises.explanation: Hoy es plus the day. Viernes still carries the name of Venus.

legacyExercises.prompt: Give the English meaning: El lunes trabajo.
legacyExercises.explanation: There is no separate word for on here; the article el does that work in front of the day.

legacyExercises.prompt: Five Spanish weekdays carry the name of a planet or a god. Which pair leaves that company?
legacyExercises.explanation: Sábado comes from the Sabbath and domingo from the Lord's day; lunes to viernes are the old sky names.

legacyExercises.prompt: Read the week. Which day does the passage name after the moon?
legacyExercises.explanation: The first line says it: el lunes is the day of la Luna, the moon.
legacyExercises.passage: El lunes es el día de la Luna. El martes trabajo. El miércoles estudio. El jueves llamo a mi madre. El viernes descanso.
legacyExercises.translation: Monday is the day of the moon. On Tuesday I work. On Wednesday I study. On Thursday I call my mother. On Friday I rest.

lessons.culturalNote: Spanish weekdays are not capitalised, which is why lunes looks the same mid-sentence as at the start of one.

lessons.title: Family and people
lessons.objective: Say how many brothers and sisters you have, and let mi or mis follow the number you name.
lessons.culturalNote: Familia in Spanish often stretches to grandparents, aunts and cousins, not just the household.

lessons.title: Build it: polite requests
lessons.objective: Build polite café requests from their parts, without looking at the frame.

lessons.title: Mission: find the café
lessons.objective: Ask the way to the café, follow directions, and order politely.

lessons.title: Remember the basics
lessons.objective: Retrieve words and phrases from your first four lessons, from memory.

lessons.title: Mission: find the museum
lessons.objective: Ask the way to the museum, buy a ticket, and say thanks.

lessons.title: Mission: the birthday party
lessons.objective: Greet the host, introduce yourself, and introduce your brother and sister.

lessons.title: Build it: my family
lessons.objective: Build sentences about your family from tiles.

lessons.title: Home and articles
lessons.objective: Name the rooms of a home and put the right article — el, la, los, las — in front of every noun.
lessons.culturalNote: Many Spanish homes centre on the salón, the living room where the family eats, talks and watches television together.

lessons.title: Describing things
lessons.objective: Describe things with ser and make the adjective match — alto with el libro, alta with la casa.

legacyExercises.prompt: Mesa is feminine. Which line describes it correctly?
legacyExercises.explanation: Mesa is feminine and singular, so both the article and the adjective stay feminine: la mesa es nueva.

legacyExercises.prompt: Predict the sentence before you write it: the house is big.
legacyExercises.explanation: Casa is feminine, but grande is one of the adjectives that doesn't change for gender — only for number: La casa es grande.

legacyExercises.prompt: Muy always stands right before the adjective. Choose the correct line.
legacyExercises.explanation: Muy hugs the adjective it strengthens: es muy alto.

legacyExercises.prompt: Put the words in order: the house is very big.
legacyExercises.explanation: Ser carries the description, and muy stands before grande: La casa es muy grande.

legacyExercises.prompt: Translate into Spanish: They are tall. (masculine)
legacyExercises.explanation: Ser in the plural is son, and alto copies the masculine plural: Son altos.

legacyExercises.prompt: Libro is masculine and singular. Fill the gap: El libro es ___.
legacyExercises.explanation: Libro is masculine and singular, so the adjective stays nuevo: El libro es nuevo.

legacyExercises.prompt: Read the description. Which adjective describes the lamp?
legacyExercises.explanation: The last sentence gives it: la lámpara es alta.
legacyExercises.passage: Mi dormitorio es pequeño pero bonito. La cama es nueva y la mesa es grande. El libro de la mesa es muy interesante. La lámpara es alta.
legacyExercises.translation: My bedroom is small but pretty. The bed is new and the table is big. The book on the table is very interesting. The lamp is tall.

lessons.culturalNote: Spanish puts most adjectives after the noun — la casa grande — which is why the description always comes last.

lessons.title: More than one
lessons.objective: Make plurals the Spanish way — add -s after a vowel, -es after a consonant.
lessons.culturalNote: Spanish plurals are wonderfully regular compared to English: no mice or children to memorise, just -s and -es.

lessons.title: Work and daily routine
lessons.objective: Talk about your day with trabajar and estudiar, and place it with por la mañana, por la tarde, por la noche.
lessons.culturalNote: In Spain the working day often pauses for a long midday break, so por la tarde can start surprisingly late.

lessons.title: Saying no
lessons.objective: Say no and not in Spanish — no goes right before the verb — and add nunca, nada and nadie.
lessons.culturalNote: Spanish happily doubles its negatives — No como nada — where English would call it a double negative.

lessons.title: Asking questions
lessons.objective: Ask with qué, quién, dónde, cuándo and cómo — and remember the accent marks.
lessons.culturalNote: Spanish writes the question twice — ¿ at the start and ? at the end — so the reader hears the question coming.

lessons.title: Food and drink
lessons.objective: Talk about food with comer and beber, and say what you like with me gusta.
lessons.culturalNote: In Spain lunch is the big meal of the day, often eaten well after 2 p.m.

lessons.title: Mine and yours
lessons.objective: Say whose it is with mi, tu and su — and make them plural with mis, tus, sus.
lessons.culturalNote: Spanish skips the article before a possessive — mi casa, not la mi casa.

lessons.title: Getting around
lessons.objective: Say how you get around with ir — voy, vas, va — and en coche, en metro, a pie.
lessons.culturalNote: Spanish cities run on the metro and on foot; a pie is a point of pride, not a fallback.

lessons.title: Polite requests
lessons.objective: Ask politely with poder and querer — and soften everything with querría.
lessons.culturalNote: Querría turns a demand into a request; in a Spanish bar it is the difference between ordering and asking.

lessons.title: Yesterday: a first look at the past
lessons.objective: Take a first step into the past with hablé, comí — and the mighty fue.

legacyExercises.prompt: Which line says I spoke with Ana yesterday?
legacyExercises.explanation: The -é ending with its accent is the I form of the past: Ayer hablé con Ana.

legacyExercises.prompt: Predict the sentence before you write it: I ate bread.
legacyExercises.explanation: Comer is an -er verb, so the I past ends in -í: Comí pan.

legacyExercises.prompt: Fue means was here. Choose the correct line.
legacyExercises.explanation: Fue already means was — no helper verb needed: La película fue muy buena.
options: La película es fue muy buena.
La película era fue muy buena.

legacyExercises.prompt: Put the words in order: last night I studied Spanish.
legacyExercises.explanation: Time first, then the past verb: Anoche estudié español.

legacyExercises.prompt: Translate into Spanish: Yesterday I worked a lot.
legacyExercises.explanation: Ayer sets the past, and trabajé carries the accent: Ayer trabajé mucho.

legacyExercises.prompt: The subject is yo, so the past of hablar ends in -é. Fill the gap: Ayer ___ con mi madre.
legacyExercises.explanation: The I past of hablar is hablé: Ayer hablé con mi madre.

legacyExercises.prompt: Read about yesterday. Who did the writer speak with?
legacyExercises.explanation: The third sentence names her: hablé con Ana.
legacyExercises.passage: Ayer fue un día perfecto. Comí con mi familia. Por la tarde hablé con Ana. Anoche estudié un poco y dormí bien.
legacyExercises.translation: Yesterday was a perfect day. I ate with my family. In the afternoon I spoke with Ana. Last night I studied a little and slept well.

lessons.culturalNote: Spanish tells stories in the past tense the way English does — once you have hablé and fue, anecdotes open up.

lessons.title: Making plans
lessons.objective: Talk about the near future the easy way — ir a plus the infinitive.
lessons.culturalNote: Spanish plans the near future with going-to, just like English — voy a viajar feels instantly familiar.

lessons.title: Weather and seasons
lessons.objective: Talk about the weather with hace sol, hace frío — and name the four seasons.
lessons.culturalNote: Spaniards discuss the weather with hacer — to make — as if the sky were cooking it up.

lessons.title: Telling the time
lessons.objective: Tell the time — Es la una, Son las tres y media — and ask ¿Qué hora es?
lessons.culturalNote: Spain runs famously late — dinner at ten is normal, so telling the time matters.

lessons.title: Months and dates
lessons.objective: Name the months and give dates the Spanish way — el 3 de mayo.

legacyExercises.prompt: Which line writes the date correctly?
legacyExercises.explanation: The day needs its el and the month its de: el 3 de mayo.

legacyExercises.prompt: Predict the sentence before you write it: my birthday is in June.
legacyExercises.explanation: For the month alone, en is enough: Mi cumpleaños es en junio.

legacyExercises.prompt: Months stay lowercase. Choose the correct line.
legacyExercises.explanation: Diciembre never takes a capital: La fiesta es en diciembre.
options: La fiesta es en el diciembre.

answers: Mi cumpleaños es el cinco de enero.
legacyExercises.prompt: Put the words in order: my birthday is January 5th.
legacyExercises.explanation: El 5 de enero — day first: Mi cumpleaños es el cinco de enero.

answers: Hoy es el tres de mayo.
legacyExercises.prompt: Translate into Spanish: Today is May 3rd.
legacyExercises.explanation: Day with el, month with de: Hoy es el tres de mayo.

legacyExercises.prompt: The month is June, always lowercase. Fill the gap: El concierto es el 20 de ___.
legacyExercises.explanation: Lowercase, as always: El concierto es el 20 de junio.

legacyExercises.prompt: Read the birthday note. When is the writer's birthday?
legacyExercises.explanation: The first sentence gives the date: el 5 de enero.
legacyExercises.passage: Mi cumpleaños es el 5 de enero. La fiesta es el 10 de enero en mi casa. Mi hermana cumple en junio. Mis padres cumplen en diciembre.
legacyExercises.translation: My birthday is January 5th. The party is January 10th at my house. My sister's birthday is in June. My parents' birthdays are in December.

lessons.culturalNote: Spanish months stay lowercase, even mid-sentence — mayo, never Mayo.

lessons.title: At the market
lessons.objective: Buy by quantity — un kilo de, una botella de — and point with este and esta.
lessons.culturalNote: Spanish markets sell by the kilo and the half-kilo; medio kilo is the everyday unit.

lessons.title: Free time and hobbies
lessons.objective: Say what you love doing — Me gusta leer, Me encanta nadar.
lessons.culturalNote: El fútbol is practically a religion in Spain; juego al fútbol will start conversations anywhere.

lessons.title: Health and the body
lessons.objective: Name body parts and say what hurts — Me duele la cabeza.
lessons.culturalNote: Spanish pharmacies are the first stop for minor ailments; the pharmacist advises before the doctor does.

lessons.title: At the pharmacy
lessons.objective: Ask for what you need at the pharmacy — Necesito algo para el dolor.
lessons.culturalNote: In Spain many medicines need no prescription — es sin receta is a phrase worth knowing.

lessons.title: Emergencies
lessons.objective: Handle emergencies — ¡Socorro!, Llame a una ambulancia, ¿Dónde está el hospital?

legacyExercises.prompt: Which line gives the formal command to call an ambulance?
legacyExercises.explanation: Llame is the formal command, and llamar needs its a: Llame a una ambulancia.

legacyExercises.prompt: Predict the question before you write it: where is the hospital?
legacyExercises.explanation: Dónde with its accent, está for location: ¿Dónde está el hospital?

legacyExercises.prompt: Emergencies use the formal command. Choose the correct cry.
legacyExercises.explanation: Llame is the usted command — Llamo would mean I call, which helps nobody.

answers: Llame a una ambulancia, por favor.
legacyExercises.prompt: Put the words in order: call an ambulance, please.
legacyExercises.explanation: The command first, then a una ambulancia: Llame a una ambulancia, por favor.

legacyExercises.prompt: Translate into Spanish: I need help!
legacyExercises.explanation: Necesito ayuda, with the marks that frame it: ¡Necesito ayuda!

legacyExercises.prompt: This is the cry for help. Fill the gap: ¡___!
legacyExercises.explanation: ¡Socorro! is the cry for help.

legacyExercises.prompt: Read the emergency. What does the woman call?
legacyExercises.explanation: The second sentence says it: llama a una ambulancia.
legacyExercises.passage: Hay una emergencia. Un hombre grita: ¡Socorro! Una mujer llama a una ambulancia. La ambulancia llega rápido. El hombre está bien.
legacyExercises.translation: There is an emergency. A man shouts: Help! A woman calls an ambulance. The ambulance arrives quickly. The man is fine.

lessons.culturalNote: 112 is the Europe-wide emergency number, and it works everywhere in Spain.

lessons.title: Invitations
lessons.objective: Invite, accept and decline — Te invito a cenar, ¡Claro que sí!, Lo siento, no puedo.
lessons.culturalNote: Spaniards often confirm plans at the last minute; no news before the party is usually good news.

lessons.title: Formar el pretérito
lessons.objective: Build the past tense: full -ar/-er/-ir endings and the big irregulars.

legacyExercises.prompt: Which ending marks the yo form of -ar verbs in the past?
legacyExercises.explanation: trabajé — the é is the I-did-it marker. trabajo is present (I work), trabaja is he/she present, trabajar is the untouched infinitive.

legacyExercises.prompt: Predict the yo past of comer: Yesterday I ate → Ayer ___ .
legacyExercises.explanation: -er/-ir verbs take -í for yo: comí. Keep the accent — comi without it is a spelling mistake, not a past tense.

legacyExercises.prompt: Estuvo enfermo ayer. Which verb is the rebel here?
legacyExercises.explanation: estuvo — estar's past ignores the -ar pattern completely (no *estó). enfermo is an adjective, ayer a time word, and fue isn't even in the sentence.

legacyExercises.prompt: Put the words in order: We ate paella on Sunday.
legacyExercises.explanation: Comimos paella el domingo — verb first, then what, then when. The past verb carries the whole sentence.

legacyExercises.prompt: Translate into Spanish: He told me no.
legacyExercises.explanation: decir → dijo in the past — one of the rebels. Me dijo que no: told-me that no.

legacyExercises.prompt: Anoche ___ la tarea. (hacer, yo)
legacyExercises.explanation: hacer → hice. The yo past of hacer drops the pattern — memorize hice the way you memorized fue.

legacyExercises.prompt: Read the day. What time did the narrator get home?
legacyExercises.explanation: Llegué a casa a las once — the last pretérito of the story, and your answer.
legacyExercises.passage: Ayer fue un día largo. Me levanté a las siete, desayuné café con tostadas y salí a trabajar. Por la tarde hablé con mi jefe y terminé el informe. Por la noche cené con amigos y llegué a casa a las once.
legacyExercises.translation: Yesterday was a long day. I got up at seven, had coffee with toast for breakfast and left for work. In the afternoon I spoke with my boss and finished the report. At night I had dinner with friends and got home at eleven.

lessons.culturalNote: In Spain the pretérito perfecto (he hablado) covers the recent past; across much of Latin America the simple pretérito (hablé) does that job too. Both are understood everywhere — pick one and stay consistent.

lessons.title: El imperfecto
lessons.objective: Use the imperfecto for habits, settings and background scenes.
lessons.culturalNote: Storytellers in Spanish love the imperfecto for scene-setting — novels open with era, había, llovía. Listen for it in any story and you will feel the scene slow down around you.

lessons.title: Pretérito o imperfecto
lessons.objective: Choose the right past: pretérito for events, imperfecto for background.
lessons.culturalNote: Spanish speakers mix both pasts in one breath — Hacía sol y de repente llovió. Mastering the switch is the moment your Spanish starts sounding natural instead of translated.

lessons.title: Contar el fin de semana
lessons.objective: Tell your weekend in the past: sequence words and past verbs.
lessons.culturalNote: ¿Qué hiciste el fin de semana? is the Monday-morning question everywhere in the Spanish-speaking world — offices, schools, bars. This lesson hands you the answer.

lessons.title: Formar el futuro
lessons.objective: Form the simple future: infinitive + endings, plus the rebel stems.

legacyExercises.prompt: How is the simple future formed?
legacyExercises.explanation: infinitive + endings: hablar + é = hablaré. -aba is the imperfecto; the infinitive stays whole — nothing is removed.

legacyExercises.prompt: Predict the yo future of comer.
legacyExercises.explanation: comer + é = comeré. Same ending for -ar, -er and -ir — the future doesn't care about verb groups.

legacyExercises.prompt: Which verb keeps a normal stem in the future?
legacyExercises.explanation: hablaré — hablar is regular. tener→tendré, poder→podré and decir→diré are three of the six rebel stems.

legacyExercises.prompt: Put the words in order: Tomorrow I will speak with him.
legacyExercises.explanation: Mañana hablaré con él — when, what, with whom. The future verb carries the promise.

legacyExercises.prompt: Translate into Spanish: We will eat at two.
legacyExercises.explanation: comer + emos = comeremos. The nosotros ending is the only one with the stress on the ending's first syllable.

legacyExercises.prompt: El viernes ___ a cenar. (salir, nosotros)
legacyExercises.explanation: salir → saldr-: saldremos. The d sneaks in — one of the six rebels.

legacyExercises.prompt: Read the week ahead. When will the narrator travel to Barcelona?
legacyExercises.explanation: el martes viajaré — the future verb plus its day. Plans wear dates.
legacyExercises.passage: La próxima semana será intensa. El lunes tendré una reunión importante y el martes viajaré a Barcelona. El miércoles haré una presentación y el jueves podré descansar. El viernes saldremos a cenar para celebrar.
legacyExercises.translation: Next week will be intense. On Monday I will have an important meeting and on Tuesday I will travel to Barcelona. On Wednesday I will give a presentation and on Thursday I will be able to rest. On Friday we will go out to dinner to celebrate.

lessons.culturalNote: In speech, many speakers prefer ir a + infinitive (voy a viajar) for personal plans — but the simple future owns predictions, promises and formal plans. Know both, and you will hear the difference in register.

lessons.title: Usos del futuro
lessons.objective: Use the future for promises, predictions and present guesses.
lessons.culturalNote: ¿Será verdad? — I wonder if it's true? The future of supposition softens questions into wonderings and is everywhere in conversation. It is also how weather forecasts speak: Mañana lloverá.

lessons.title: Planes e intenciones
lessons.objective: State plans with ir a + infinitive and wishes with querer.

legacyExercises.prompt: Which sentence states a decided plan?
legacyExercises.explanation: Voy a = decided and happening. quizá = maybe; estudiaba = used to; estudié = finished. Only ir a carries a live plan.

legacyExercises.prompt: Predict: you (tú) are going to come → ___ a venir.
legacyExercises.explanation: ir gives vas for tú — vas a venir. The a is the bridge; the second verb never changes.

legacyExercises.prompt: Vamos a comprar una casa. Who is 'we'?
legacyExercises.explanation: vamos = we (nosotros) — the plan includes me. The ending -amos is the giveaway.

legacyExercises.prompt: Put the words in order: I am going to learn Italian.
legacyExercises.explanation: Voy a aprender italiano — conjugated ir, then a, then the untouched infinitive. That order never changes.

legacyExercises.prompt: Translate into Spanish: We are going to travel in summer.
legacyExercises.explanation: Vamos a viajar — we-plan in four syllables. En verano pins down when.

legacyExercises.prompt: ___ a venir a la fiesta? (tú, are you going to…)
legacyExercises.explanation: ¿Vas a venir? — the invitation check. Vas, not *voy: the plan is theirs, not yours.

legacyExercises.prompt: Read the life plan. Who is going to live with the narrator?
legacyExercises.explanation: Mi hermana va a venir a vivir conmigo — va a, the third-person plan.
legacyExercises.passage: El próximo año voy a cambiar mi vida. Voy a buscar un trabajo nuevo y voy a aprender italiano. Mi hermana va a venir a vivir conmigo y vamos a viajar juntas en verano. Son planes grandes, pero tengo la intención de cumplirlos.
legacyExercises.translation: Next year I am going to change my life. I am going to look for a new job and I am going to learn Italian. My sister is going to come live with me and we are going to travel together in summer. They are big plans, but I intend to keep them.

lessons.culturalNote: New Year's resolutions across the Spanish-speaking world start with Este año voy a… — say it out loud and the plan feels real. Voy a is also how friends make weekend plans on the spot.

lessons.title: El condicional
lessons.objective: Use the conditional for wishes, advice and polite requests.
lessons.culturalNote: ¿Podrías…? opens every polite request in Spanish — sharper than the imperative, warmer than a plain question. It is the single most useful verb form a traveler can own.

lessons.title: Cortesía: me gustaría, quisiera
lessons.objective: Ask politely: me gustaría, quisiera and the manners that open doors.
lessons.culturalNote: In Spain and Latin America a softened request gets a warmer answer — Quisiera is the traveler's magic word in every restaurant, shop and hotel. Pair it with por favor and perdona and you will never sound demanding.

lessons.title: Quiero que…: el subjuntivo
lessons.objective: Trigger the subjunctive with quiero que, necesito que, es importante que.

answers: a wish on someone else triggers the subjunctive
legacyExercises.prompt: Quiero que vengas. Why vengas and not vienes?
legacyExercises.explanation: a wish on someone else — quiero que flips the second verb into the subjunctive. Same subject would stay infinitive: Quiero venir.
options: a wish on someone else triggers the subjunctive

legacyExercises.prompt: Predict the subjunctive: quiero que ___ (hablar, tú).
legacyExercises.explanation: hablo → hable → hables: drop the -o, add the opposite ending, then the tú -s. The recipe never changes.

legacyExercises.prompt: Which trigger needs the subjunctive?
legacyExercises.explanation: quiero que — wanting triggers it. creer, saber and es verdad keep the indicative: Creo que viene (fact, not wish).

legacyExercises.prompt: Put the words in order: I need you to help me.
legacyExercises.explanation: Necesito que me ayudes — the need, the que-bridge, then the subjunctive. Word order is mercifully simple.

legacyExercises.prompt: Translate into Spanish: It's important that you study. (tú)
legacyExercises.explanation: Es importante que estudies — the impersonal trigger works exactly like quiero que.

legacyExercises.prompt: Quiero que ___ a la fiesta. (venir, tú)
legacyExercises.explanation: Quiero que vengas — venir's subjunctive is irregular (veng-), but the trigger is perfectly regular.

legacyExercises.prompt: Read the mother's rules. How many hours of sleep does she want?
legacyExercises.explanation: es importante que duermas ocho horas — the subjunctive duermas carries the mother's wish.
legacyExercises.passage: Mi madre siempre dice lo mismo: quiero que estudies, necesito que me ayudes en casa y es importante que duermas ocho horas. Yo quiero que me deje en paz, pero sé que tiene razón. Quiero que sea feliz, así que la ayudo.
legacyExercises.translation: My mother always says the same thing: I want you to study, I need you to help me at home and it's important that you sleep eight hours. I want her to leave me alone, but I know she's right. I want her to be happy, so I help her.

lessons.culturalNote: The subjunctive is the mood of wishes, doubts and feelings — the moment you use it, your Spanish stops sounding like a phrasebook and starts sounding like a person. Natives notice it instantly.

lessons.title: Que, quien, donde
lessons.objective: Link clauses with que, quien/quienes, donde, el que and lo que.
lessons.culturalNote: Relative clauses let you pack a whole story into one sentence — the difference between pointing at things and actually describing your world. Fluent speakers glue constantly; learners list.

lessons.title: Comparativos
lessons.objective: Compare with más/menos…que, tan…como, mejor/peor.

answers: Es tan alto como su hermano.
legacyExercises.prompt: Which sentence compares two things as equal?
legacyExercises.explanation: tan…como = as…as — equality. más/menos…que compare unequally; el más alto crowns him above all.
options: Es tan alto como su hermano.
Es más alto que su hermano.
Es menos alto que su hermano.

legacyExercises.prompt: Predict: better → ___.
legacyExercises.explanation: mejor — bueno's rebel form. Never *más bueno; the rebel replaces the formula.

answers: before a number, que becomes de
legacyExercises.prompt: Más de tres personas. Why de and not que?
legacyExercises.explanation: before a number, que becomes de: más de tres, menos de diez. Numbers get their own preposition.
options: before a number, que becomes de

answers: Madrid es más grande que Sevilla.
legacyExercises.prompt: Put the words in order: Madrid is bigger than Seville.
legacyExercises.explanation: Madrid es más grande que Sevilla — the formula in order: noun, es, más, adjective, que, rival.

answers: Mi piso es menos caro que el tuyo.
legacyExercises.prompt: Translate into Spanish: My flat is less expensive than yours.
legacyExercises.explanation: menos caro que — less follows the same formula as more. El tuyo = yours, no noun repeated.

legacyExercises.prompt: Es ___ alto como su hermano. (as…)
legacyExercises.explanation: tan…como — the equality pair. Tan opens it, como closes it.

legacyExercises.prompt: Read the brothers. Who cooks better?
legacyExercises.explanation: cocino mejor que él — I cook better than him. Mejor settles the kitchen debate.
legacyExercises.passage: Mi hermano y yo somos muy diferentes. Él es más alto que yo y corre más rápido. Yo soy menos deportista, pero cocino mejor que él. Nuestra madre dice que somos tan tercos como nuestro padre. En el fondo, nos queremos más que a nadie.
legacyExercises.translation: My brother and I are very different. He is taller than me and runs faster. I am less sporty, but I cook better than him. Our mother says we are as stubborn as our father. Deep down, we love each other more than anyone.

lessons.culturalNote: Comparisons fuel friendly debate — ¿Cuál es mejor? starts conversations in every bar in Spain. Have an opinion, defend it with tan…como, and you are in.

lessons.title: Pronombres: lo, la, le
lessons.objective: Swap nouns for lo/la/le/les and combine them into se lo.
lessons.culturalNote: Pronouns are the oil of Spanish conversation — natives drop nouns constantly. Lo vi, se lo dije: short, fast, natural. Repeating the noun every time marks you as a beginner instantly.

lessons.title: Por y para
lessons.objective: Split por (cause, through) from para (purpose, deadline).

legacyExercises.prompt: Estudio para aprender. Para here marks…
legacyExercises.explanation: purpose — para aprender = in order to learn, the goal ahead. Causes and movement belong to por.

legacyExercises.prompt: Predict: Thanks for your help → gracias ___ tu ayuda.
legacyExercises.explanation: gracias por — por looks back at what you're thankful for. The help already happened.

legacyExercises.prompt: Lo hice por ti. Por here means…
legacyExercises.explanation: because of you — por ti names the cause behind the action. The recipient reading (*for you as destination) would be para ti.

legacyExercises.prompt: Put the words in order: It's for you.
legacyExercises.explanation: Es para ti — the recipient gets para. Three words, one direction: forward.

legacyExercises.prompt: Translate into Spanish: I need it for tomorrow.
legacyExercises.explanation: para mañana — the deadline reading of para. By tomorrow, not because of tomorrow.

legacyExercises.prompt: Paso ___ Madrid para ver a mi hermana. (through…)
legacyExercises.explanation: por Madrid = through Madrid — movement through space. Then para ver: the purpose of the stop.

legacyExercises.prompt: Read the trip. When does the narrator return?
legacyExercises.explanation: Vuelvo el lunes por la noche — por la noche is por's time-of-day reading: in/during the night.
legacyExercises.passage: Mañana salgo de viaje por trabajo. Paso por Madrid para ver a mi hermana y después sigo para Barcelona. Llevo este regalo para ella y una carta para su jefe. Lo hago por cariño: para mí, la familia es lo primero. Vuelvo el lunes por la noche.
legacyExercises.translation: Tomorrow I leave on a work trip. I pass through Madrid to see my sister and then continue to Barcelona. I'm bringing this gift for her and a letter for her boss. I do it out of affection: for me, family comes first. I return Monday night.

lessons.culturalNote: Por vs para is the classic learner headache — but natives hear the logic instantly: por explains, para intends. Get the direction right (backward vs forward) and you are understood even when you hesitate.

lessons.title: Superlativos y el trabajo
lessons.objective: Crown the best with el más… and -ísimo; talk about work.

answers: Es el más alto de la clase.
legacyExercises.prompt: Which sentence is a superlative?
legacyExercises.explanation: Es el más alto de la clase — el más…de crowns him above all. más…que only compares two; tan…como declares equality.
options: Es el más alto de la clase.

legacyExercises.prompt: Predict the -ísimo form of bueno.
legacyExercises.explanation: bueno → buenísimo: drop the -o, weld on -ísimo. Extreme good, one word.

legacyExercises.prompt: La oficina es grandísima. Grandísima means…
legacyExercises.explanation: huge — -ísima cranks grande to the extreme. It's not a diminutive; it's a megaphone.

legacyExercises.prompt: Put the words in order: I have an interview tomorrow.
legacyExercises.explanation: Tengo una entrevista mañana — have, what, when. The job hunt in four words.

legacyExercises.prompt: Translate into Spanish: My schedule is flexible.
legacyExercises.explanation: Mi horario es flexible — el horario, masculine. States of things wear ser.

legacyExercises.prompt: Mis compañeros son ___ más amables del mundo.
legacyExercises.explanation: los — the article must match compañeros (masculine plural). El más…de needs its article to agree.

legacyExercises.prompt: Read the new job. How many days a week does the narrator work?
legacyExercises.explanation: trabajo cuatro días por semana — and calls the schedule buenísimo. The superlative earns its keep.
legacyExercises.passage: Mi trabajo nuevo es el mejor que he tenido. La oficina es grandísima y está en el centro. Mi jefe es exigente pero justo, y mis compañeros son los más amables del mundo. El sueldo no es altísimo, pero el horario es buenísimo: trabajo cuatro días por semana.
legacyExercises.translation: My new job is the best I've had. The office is huge and it's downtown. My boss is demanding but fair, and my colleagues are the kindest in the world. The salary isn't super high, but the schedule is great: I work four days a week.

lessons.culturalNote: Job interviews in Spanish love superlatives — Soy el más adecuado para el puesto. Confidence, grammatically delivered, in the language employers actually hear.

lessons.title: Misión: en el hotel
lessons.objective: Check into a hotel: greet, confirm your booking, ask about breakfast, report a problem.

lessons.title: Tecnología
lessons.objective: Handle tech in Spanish: passwords, screens, sending and downloading.

legacyExercises.prompt: Which sentence asks for the wifi password?
legacyExercises.explanation: ¿Cuál es…? asks which one it is — the password itself. Dónde asks where, qué asks what it is, cuánto asks the price.

legacyExercises.prompt: Predict the yo present of enviar: te ___ un mensaje.
legacyExercises.explanation: enviar is regular: envío. Tech verbs rarely surprise you — learn the noun, the verb behaves.

legacyExercises.prompt: La contraseña del wifi. Del = …
legacyExercises.explanation: de + el — the mandatory contraction. *De el wifi is always wrong, in every register.

legacyExercises.prompt: Put the words in order: Download the app.
legacyExercises.explanation: Descarga la aplicación — command, then what. Imperatives lead with the verb.

legacyExercises.prompt: Translate into Spanish: The screen is broken.
legacyExercises.explanation: La pantalla está rota — broken states wear estar, not ser. La pantalla is feminine: rota, not roto.

legacyExercises.prompt: Te ___ el documento. (enviar, yo)
legacyExercises.explanation: Te envío — the indirect pronoun te rides before the verb: I send it to you.

legacyExercises.prompt: Read the phone saga. What did the technician say was fine?
legacyExercises.explanation: la batería está bien — está, because it's a state. The fix was the update, not the battery.
legacyExercises.passage: Ayer mi móvil dejó de funcionar. La pantalla se quedó en negro y no encendía. Fui a una tienda y el técnico me dijo: la batería está bien, pero necesitas actualizar el sistema. Descargué la actualización, encendí el móvil y funcionó. Ahora envío mensajes sin problema.
legacyExercises.translation: Yesterday my phone stopped working. The screen went black and wouldn't turn on. I went to a shop and the technician told me: the battery is fine, but you need to update the system. I downloaded the update, turned on the phone and it worked. Now I send messages without a problem.

lessons.culturalNote: ¿Tienes wifi? is the modern traveler's first question — la contraseña is the second. Tech Spanish borrows freely (el wifi, el email), so the nouns are the easy part; the verbs do the work.
